articles.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy
Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.
Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy
Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.
Comma
Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.
It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Comma is free to start and open source.
Fambot
Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.
The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.
The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.
Folk
Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Haven
Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.
According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”
Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.
Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.
Instinct
Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.
The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.
In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security.) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls.
The company remains in private beta.
Iris
Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.
Martin
Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.
It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Maverick
Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.
It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.
The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.
It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month, 20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.
Miso
Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.
It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.
Ohai
Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.
Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.
It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.
Orbits
Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.
It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.
Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.
Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.
Pally
Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.
There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.
Poke
Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.
Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.
Rene
Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.
Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.
Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.
Skye
Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.
The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.
Stanley
Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.
For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.
Szn
Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.
According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.
Tab
Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.
The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.
Tomo
The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.
Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.
The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.
Town
Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.
In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.
Underdog
Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.
The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.
Wajo
Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.
A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.
Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.
Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

articles.title: Người Nùng ở Yên Thế tìm sinh kế mới từ cây dược liệu
articles.text:
Từ những mùa vụ thua lỗ đến sinh kế mới ngay tại bản làng
Bà Liễu Thị Thơm, sinh năm 1975, người dân tộc Nùng ở bản Đồng Thép, xã Yên Thế (Bắc Ninh), từng nhiều năm chật vật tìm kế sinh nhai. Gia đình có vài nghìn mét vuông đất, trước đây chủ yếu làm ruộng, trồng vải và từng chuyển sang chăn nuôi gà với hy vọng cải thiện thu nhập.
Từ năm 1994, gia đình bà Thơm có gần 10 năm trồng vải trên đất đồi. Tuy nhiên, có thời điểm giá vải xuống chỉ còn 800-1.000 đồng/kg, tiền bán quả không đủ bù công chăm sóc. Sau đó, gia đình chuyển sang nuôi hàng nghìn con gà nhưng liên tiếp thua lỗ hai lứa do dịch bệnh và giá bán giảm sâu, có lúc chỉ còn hơn 28.000 đồng/kg.
Gia đình từng rơi vào cảnh nợ nần, phải bán đàn gà, còn bà Thơm đi làm công nhân may găng tay, quần áo tại một doanh nghiệp.
Bước ngoặt đến khi HTX Dược liệu Thiện Tâm được thành lập ngay tại địa phương. Được ông Phạm Văn Thiện, Giám đốc HTX, mời tham gia, bà Thơm trở thành thành viên và người lao động của HTX. Công việc của bà trải qua nhiều công đoạn, từ trồng, chăm sóc, thu hoạch cây dược liệu đến làm việc trong xưởng, đóng gói và chuẩn bị hàng hóa.
Theo bà Thơm, thu nhập từ công việc tại HTX tương đương khi đi làm công ty, nhưng thuận lợi hơn vì ở gần nhà. So với làm ruộng trước đây, công việc mới mang lại nguồn thu tốt hơn và đều đặn hơn. Hiện thu nhập bình quân của lao động tại HTX khoảng 10,5 triệu đồng/người/tháng.
Câu chuyện của bà Thơm phản ánh một phần thực tế sinh kế tại bản Đồng Thép, nơi có đông đồng bào dân tộc Nùng, Tày sinh sống. Theo bà, khoảng 70% người dân trong bản vẫn làm ruộng, trong khi nhiều lao động trẻ đi làm tại các khu công nghiệp ở Quang Châu, Việt Yên. Hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh tại chỗ còn hạn chế, chủ yếu có một số xưởng may nhỏ và cơ sở chế biến gỗ.
Vì vậy, sự xuất hiện của HTX dược liệu đã mở thêm cơ hội việc làm cho người dân, nhất là phụ nữ và lao động trung niên. Thay vì phải đi làm xa hoặc phụ thuộc hoàn toàn vào sản xuất nông nghiệp, họ có thể tham gia vào các công đoạn sản xuất ngay tại bản làng.
Đưa cây thuốc thành sản phẩm hàng hóa, tạo sinh kế cho người dân
Người khởi xướng mô hình là ông Phạm Văn Thiện. Với nghề thuốc gia truyền của gia đình và những kiến thức tích lũy trong quá trình công tác, ông sớm nhận thấy tiềm năng phát triển cây dược liệu tại địa phương.
Năm 2015, ông bắt đầu trồng cà gai leo, chè vằng, xạ đen, đinh lăng trên hơn 1ha đất của gia đình. Nhận thấy nếu chỉ bán cây dược liệu thô thì giá trị kinh tế chưa cao, ông quyết định đầu tư hơn 1 tỷ đồng mua máy móc, xây dựng cơ sở chế biến, chiết xuất dược liệu thành cao thành phẩm.
Khi sản phẩm được thị trường đón nhận, ông Thiện vận động các hộ dân xung quanh cùng trồng dược liệu để cung cấp nguyên liệu. Tháng 6/2019, HTX Dược liệu Thiện Tâm chính thức thành lập. Từ 15 thành viên ban đầu, đến nay HTX có 17 thành viên, tổ chức sản xuất và liên kết với người dân để phát triển vùng nguyên liệu.
Theo ông Thiện, khu vực bản Đồng Thép có điều kiện thổ nhưỡng phù hợp với nhiều loại cây dược liệu. Đất đồi thấp, khả năng thoát nước tốt cùng nguồn nước tưới từ các kênh Cẫu Rễ, kênh Tây và đập Tân Gia tạo thuận lợi cho canh tác.
Hiện HTX phát triển các loại cây như cà gai leo, đinh lăng, xạ đen, ngũ gia bì, sen nước... với tổng diện tích trồng hơn 10ha. Dược liệu sau thu hoạch được đưa về chế biến thành cao, đóng gói và phân phối ra thị trường. HTX hiện có 8 sản phẩm đạt chứng nhận OCOP 3 sao.
Không chỉ tạo đầu ra cho vùng nguyên liệu, hoạt động chế biến còn giúp HTX nâng giá trị sản phẩm và tạo thêm việc làm tại địa phương. Ba năm gần đây, doanh thu của HTX đạt hơn 1 tỷ đồng mỗi năm. HTX sử dụng 7-10 lao động mỗi ngày, trong đó có 3 lao động là người dân tộc thiểu số. Vào mùa thu hoạch, đơn vị thuê thêm nhân công thời vụ.
Sản phẩm của HTX được tiêu thụ thông qua các gian hàng của Liên minh Hợp tác xã, cửa hàng tại một số tỉnh và các kênh bán hàng trực tuyến. Đây là hướng đi giúp sản phẩm dược liệu địa phương tiếp cận thị trường rộng hơn, thay vì chỉ phụ thuộc vào việc bán nguyên liệu thô.
Tuy nhiên, để mô hình tạo sinh kế rộng hơn, việc mở rộng vùng nguyên liệu, thu hút thêm hộ dân tham gia và duy trì đầu ra ổn định vẫn là những yếu tố quan trọng. Bên cạnh đó, nâng cao chất lượng sản phẩm, phát triển thương hiệu và mở rộng thị trường cũng quyết định khả năng phát triển lâu dài của HTX.
Từ câu chuyện của bà Thơm có thể thấy, cây dược liệu có thể trở thành một hướng sản xuất tạo thêm thu nhập cho người dân khi được tổ chức trồng trọt, chế biến và tiêu thụ theo chuỗi. Với những lao động từng phải rời quê đi làm xa, mô hình này còn mở thêm cơ hội tìm việc làm ngay tại nơi sinh sống.

articles.title: Tại sao cốc, hũ thủy tinh nứt khi bạn rót nước sôi vào?
articles.text:
Thủ phạm thực sự không phải là sức nóng, mà là một hiện tượng vật lý tàn nhẫn được gọi là ứng suất nhiệt.
- Bí ẩn căn bệnh nguy hiểm hơn Ebola, không chứa vật chất di truyền nhưng có thể khiến người nhiễm bệnh chết trong những cơn cười điên dại
- Gần 70 năm trước, 26 con ong chúa đã thoát khỏi phòng thí nghiệm và tạo ra loài ong sát thủ khiến cả châu Mỹ khiếp sợ
- Thảm họa Sampoong: Trung tâm thương mại sụp đổ thành đống đổ nát chỉ trong 20 giây, lòng tham khiến gần 1.500 người bị chôn vùi
- Bên trong đường hầm đáng sợ nhất Trung Quốc: Nóng 40 độ C, nước ngầm phun như thác, 26 tháng chỉ đào được 156m đường hầm
- Hố đen ăn sạch mọi thứ, vậy những thứ bị nó nuốt chửng đã đi về đâu?
Nhiệt độ đơn thuần không bao giờ phá vỡ được thủy tinh. Chính sự thay đổi nhiệt độ quá nhanh, vượt quá tốc độ thích ứng của vật liệu, mới là nguyên nhân gây ra thảm họa. Mọi vật liệu đều giãn nở khi bị làm nóng, và thủy tinh cũng giãn ra khoảng chín phần triệu chiều dài cho mỗi độ tăng lên.
Tuy nhiên, thủy tinh lại truyền nhiệt rất chậm. Khi bạn rót nước sôi vào một chiếc hũ lạnh, lớp da bên trong lập tức nóng lên gần 100 °C, trong khi lớp da bên ngoài cách đó vài milimet vẫn ở nhiệt độ phòng. Lớp bên trong muốn giãn nở ra, nhưng những lớp dính với nó chưa nhận được nhiệt nên vẫn giữ nguyên kích thước.
Không bên nào có thể di chuyển tự do, dẫn đến việc chúng giằng xé lẫn nhau - các kỹ sư gọi đây là ứng suất nhiệt. Vết nứt xảy ra chính bởi sự khác biệt nhiệt độ xuyên qua thành hũ, chứ không phải do bản thân sức nóng của nước sôi.
Đó là lý do một chiếc hũ có thể nằm an toàn cả giờ trong nồi thanh trùng. Nó đi vào nước ấm và được làm nóng từ từ cùng với nước, khiến mọi lớp thủy tinh đều giãn nở đồng đều. Không có sự khác biệt xuyên qua thành hũ, không có lực kéo, đồng nghĩa với không có vết nứt. Nhưng khi bạn dội nước sôi trực tiếp vào hũ lạnh, nguy hiểm sẽ đạt đỉnh điểm trong những giây đầu tiên.
Thủy tinh có một đặc tính rất mất cân đối: nó chịu lực ép rất tốt nhưng lại cực kỳ yếu đuối trước lực kéo. Giới hạn chịu đựng của nó được quyết định bởi những khiếm khuyết nhỏ li ti trên bề mặt.
Mọi chiếc hũ đều có những vết xước vô hình do va chạm với bùi nhùi thép hay dao nĩa kim loại. Một vết xước đơn giản chỉ là một vết nứt chưa tới lúc bùng phát.
Khi bị làm nóng đột ngột, lớp da bên trong nở ra đẩy các bề mặt ép vào nhau, khiến các khiếm khuyết vẫn đóng lại, trong khi phần giữa thành hũ bị kéo căng.
Tuy nhiên, làm lạnh đột ngột lại mang đến một hướng tác động tàn khốc hơn. Theo các phân tích khoa học, làm lạnh khắc nghiệt hơn làm nóng đột ngột gấp ba lần. Khi hũ nóng gặp bề mặt lạnh, lớp da bên ngoài co lại ngay lập tức và bị kéo căng - đánh trúng ngay vào nơi chứa vô số vết xước hở.
Đây là lý do tại sao đặt hũ nóng lên mặt đá ướt lạnh lại nguy hiểm hơn rất nhiều so với việc dội nước nóng vào hũ ấm.
Khả năng chống chịu sốc nhiệt thay đổi tùy theo vật liệu cấu thành. Thủy tinh làm hũ mứt thông thường (soda-lime) sẽ vượt qua giới hạn chịu đựng khi gặp một bước nhảy nhiệt độ tức thời ở mức khoảng 55 °C. Một ấm nước sôi rót vào chiếc hũ ở nhiệt độ phòng tạo ra mức chênh lệch 80 °C - vượt quá xa tiêu chuẩn an toàn.
Việc chúng đôi khi vẫn sống sót chỉ là do nhiệt truyền vào thủy tinh chậm hơn so với tính toán lý thuyết, tạo ra một ván cược may rủi có thể thua chậm vài giây.
Trong khi đó, thủy tinh borosilicate nguyên bản - từng được sử dụng để làm dụng cụ nấu ăn thương hiệu Pyrex ban đầu - chỉ giãn nở ba phần triệu mỗi độ. Vật liệu này có thể chịu được bước nhảy nhiệt độ lên tới 183 °C.
Tuy nhiên, qua thời gian, nhiều đồ thủy tinh nhãn hiệu Pyrex tại Mỹ đã chuyển sang dùng thủy tinh soda-lime xử lý nhiệt, khiến biên độ an toàn chống sốc nhiệt trong nhà bếp bị thu hẹp đáng kể so với trước đây.
Làm nóng chiếc hũ trước khi rót nước sôi không phải là kinh nghiệm truyền miệng, mà là một phép toán giảm trừ ứng suất. Nếu nước vòi nóng nâng chiếc hũ từ nhiệt độ phòng lên 60 °C, mức chênh lệch khi gặp nước sôi chỉ còn 40 °C thay vì 80 °C, và ứng suất nhiệt đã giảm đi một nửa. Chiếc hũ không hề cứng hơn, vạch xuất phát nhiệt độ của nó chỉ đơn giản là được đẩy lên cao hơn.
Đây cũng là quy tắc sống còn trong việc đóng hộp thực phẩm tại nhà. Khuyến cáo từ bang Washington chỉ rõ các hũ phải được giữ nóng cho đến khi sẵn sàng đổ đầy thức ăn.
Ngược lại, để tránh làm lạnh đột ngột, hãy luôn lót một chiếc khăn khô hoặc thớt gỗ dưới hũ nóng. Chiếc khăn gấp lại chưa bao giờ nhằm mục đích giữ sạch, mà để giúp bề mặt thủy tinh không bị giảm nhiệt quá sốc.
Cuối cùng, đừng bao giờ tin tưởng tuyệt đối vào chiếc hũ chỉ vì nó từng sống sót qua nước sôi ngày hôm qua. Những vết xước trên bề mặt thủy tinh có thể lớn dần lên một chút sau mỗi lần sử dụng. Giới hạn chịu đựng của hũ thủy tinh đang mòn đi từng ngày, và chỉ cần một cú sốc nhiệt vội vã, sự kiên nhẫn của nó sẽ cạn kiệt ngay tại nơi chứa các khiếm khuyết.

articles.title: Your PC's USB port can charge your phone, even when it's turned off — Here's how - Engadget
articles.text:
Your PC's USB port can charge your phone, even when it's turned off — Here's how
Your USB ports might have a hidden "Always On" mode that charges your phone with the PC shut down.
Almost all PC USB ports supply enough current to charge a device, but not all continue to do so when the PC is shut down. This convenient feature can also be confusing, since each brand tends to have its own terminology. For example, Lenovo calls it an "Always On" port while Dell uses the term PowerShare. Others stick with icon labels, like a battery symbol or a lightning bolt. The best way to know for sure is to dig into your PC's manual, confirm the markings and learn how to enable it.
Depending on the system, USB standby power might be on by default or be part of an energy-saving setting that cuts power when the PC is off. Your desktop or motherboard documentation should have this information. Fortunately, testing the feature is fairly simple: plug your phone in, turn the PC off and see if your phone continues charging.
If it stops charging, it's safe to assume the setting is off, which you can rectify in the BIOS or UEFI on most Windows PCs. (If your PC never supported the feature, changing settings won't help.) Restart the PC and press the key the startup screen tells you to (usually F2, Del or F10). Look under Advanced, Power or Chipset for a USB power delivery or Always On charging option and enable it. If you see ErP (Energy-related Products) or Deep Sleep settings, make sure they're disabled. Save and exit.
You don't need a computer science or software engineering degree to do this, just a little patience as you wait for the PC to boot up and press the right key. The menu can be confusing at times, but you're unlikely to brick your PC.
Why your PC's USB port might stop charging after shutdown
For starters, energy-saving features may get in the way. Anything that uses standby power will conflict with firmware settings that cut power to reduce consumption. For instance, if ErP Ready is enabled in select ASUS NUC PCs, USB standby power during shutdown or hibernation is disabled. Check your system's instructions before changing anything.
You also may not have to turn off every single energy-saving feature just to charge your phone when your PC is off. Keep in mind that changing the energy-saving settings won't add post-shutdown charging if the system never supported it to begin with.
Laptops are an entirely different case, since they often come with battery reserve limitations. Depending on the model, USB charging may stop when the laptop's battery hits a reserve threshold. Laptop charging features may depend on an AC adapter after shutdown, and that's a potential restriction that shouldn't be confused with a desktop's standby power settings. Make sure your USB plug is completely in the port and that the cable is reliable, not one that's been sitting in an attic box for the last quarter century.
What does it mean when a USB port is Always On?
In this context, "Always On" refers to power availability, but that's not the same thing as "charging only." A supported port can continue to supply power while the computer is off, though the wording shouldn't be taken literally. Firmware settings can disable that power, and the behavior may be different between ports on the same system.
Power and data transfers are also different capabilities. A phone charging while the PC is shut down doesn't mean you can transfer photos from your phone or copy files to it. The specific feature here is all about electricity available via the USB connection.
Another problem is the lack of consistency in names, setup processes and USB port symbols. One system may offer a dedicated USB power setting while another's ports depend on power-saving configurations. Even within a single brand, capabilities and terminology can differ, and manufacturers implement "Always On" USB in drastically different ways.
For example, "Always On" could mean the feature is active after shutdown, during hibernation or while your PC is asleep. It could mean two of them, just one or all three. The feature may come with symbols, color coding, terminology or fine print in a manual, but not necessarily all of the above.

articles.title: The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore
articles.text:
On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.
“The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”
Monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.
The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.
“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.
“And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”
I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.
Cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that says “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.
The house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: New Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.
These guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.
Part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is currently facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.
During the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he says, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”
Of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.
“I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”
This is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole says.
Of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole says.
In selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.
I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.)
I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.
Later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon says afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”
Cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he says, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.)
The next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.
“It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.
If they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy says.
The Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.
Instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones said. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”
Even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—quickly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he says. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”
The bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole says embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then shows a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.
Then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.
“Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright says. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”
Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.
“I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been said offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he says. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”
The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”
The vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”
“In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's important to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.
Immediately, someone says that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”
Echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he says.
The tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright says he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”
Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation said that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.
He isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).
Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he says. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”
All told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.
Little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, says some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.
But there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.
There was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel shows Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.
I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he said. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

articles.title: Các ông lớn cà phê đua săn mặt bằng đẹp, có nơi giá thuê gần 400 triệu đồng/tháng
articles.text:
Mặt bằng gần 400 triệu đồng/tháng
Sau khoảng 8 năm hoạt động, một nhà hàng quy mô lớn tại Hai Bà Trưng, Hà Nội, đã dừng kinh doanh và trả lại mặt bằng từ 9/11. Mặt bằng rộng khoảng 700m2, nằm ở ngã ba góc giao giữa phố Lê Đại Hành và Mai Hắc Đế. Theo thông tin từ chủ hệ thống, giá thuê tại đây từng ở mức 200 triệu đồng/tháng, sau nhiều năm tăng lên 385 triệu đồng/tháng.
Một thương hiệu cà phê được cho là đã thuê lại mặt bằng ngã ba này.
Thực tế tại Hà Nội cho thấy, các chuỗi cà phê không chỉ tìm kiếm địa điểm kinh doanh có khả năng sinh lời trực tiếp. Những vị trí nổi bật, đông người qua lại còn có giá trị trong việc quảng bá và định vị thương hiệu.
Cuối tháng 8/2026, thị trường F&B tại Hà Nội chú ý đến sự xuất hiện của cửa hàng mới thuộc chuỗi Phúc Long tại số 87 Đinh Tiên Hoàng. Nằm trong khuôn viên tòa nhà Bưu điện Hà Nội, ngay sát hồ Hoàn Kiếm, cửa hàng có diện tích khoảng 360m2. Đây là một trong những vị trí kinh doanh đắc địa, sở hữu tầm nhìn trực diện ra hồ Gươm và lượng người qua lại lớn.
Phúc Long mở cửa hàng tại cùng tòa nhà Bưu điện Hà Nội, nơi Starbucks đã hiện diện từ trước. Khu vực này còn có sự góp mặt của Highlands Coffee và một số thương hiệu đồ uống khác, tạo nên cụm kinh doanh F&B tại vị trí trung tâm Thủ đô.
Mức giá thuê cụ thể của mặt bằng chưa được công bố. Với diện tích lớn và vị trí đặc biệt đắc địa, chi phí thuê được giới kinh doanh dự đoán có thể lên tới hàng trăm triệu đồng mỗi tháng.
Tại Hà Nội, Highlands Coffee đang đứng đầu về quy mô và độ phủ với khoảng hơn 200 điểm bán. Chuỗi này hiện diện tại nhiều vị trí đông dân cư, các nút giao thông lớn, chân đế tòa nhà văn phòng và trung tâm thương mại.
Phúc Long hiện có khoảng 41 điểm bán. Dù số lượng cửa hàng chưa thể so sánh với Highlands, thương hiệu này đang chú trọng những mặt bằng có khả năng tạo dấu ấn.
Phê La và Katinat cũng nổi lên như những đối thủ đáng chú ý trong cuộc đua mặt bằng đẹp. Phê La hiện có khoảng 30 cửa hàng tại Hà Nội. Nhiều cửa hàng của chuỗi này lựa chọn mặt bằng có không gian thoáng, chú trọng thiết kế và trải nghiệm.
Katinat có khoảng 17 cửa hàng tại Hà Nội, trên tổng quy mô hơn 125 điểm bán toàn quốc. Một số cửa hàng Katinat được đặt tại các vị trí góc phố, có khả năng nhận diện từ nhiều hướng.
Trong khi đó, Starbucks theo đuổi chiến lược hiện diện tại những địa điểm có tính biểu tượng như Bưu điện Hà Nội, Nhà thờ Lớn hay khu vực phố Lý Thái Tổ. Tại Hà Nội, Starbucks có khoảng 35 cửa hàng.
Cuộc chơi tiền tỷ của các chuỗi cà phê
Đằng sau những cửa hàng sáng đèn tại các tuyến phố trung tâm là bài toán chi phí mặt bằng không nhỏ.
Tại các tuyến phố như Đinh Tiên Hoàng, Hàng Bài, Tràng Tiền và Lê Thái Tổ, giá thuê dao động khoảng 100-250 USD/m2/tháng, tương đương 2,5-6,5 triệu đồng/m2/tháng. Với diện tích 150-350m2, tiền thuê mặt bằng có thể lên tới hàng trăm triệu đồng mỗi tháng.
Tại các tuyến phố như Lý Thường Kiệt, Hai Bà Trưng, Bà Triệu, Lê Đại Hành, giá thuê phổ biến khoảng 50-100 USD/m2/tháng, tương đương 1,3-2,6 triệu đồng/m2/tháng. Với những mặt bằng góc hai mặt tiền, tiền thuê mỗi tháng có thể lên tới hàng trăm triệu đồng.
Ngay cả các khu vực ngoài trung tâm như Cầu Giấy, Đống Đa và Thanh Xuân, những mặt bằng có vị trí đẹp, diện tích lớn và khả năng kinh doanh tốt cũng được nhiều thương hiệu săn đón.
Dù mức giá thuê cao, các chuỗi kinh doanh vẫn sẵn sàng chi đậm để chiếm lĩnh các mặt bằng đắc địa. Một chủ chuỗi nhà hàng từng chia sẻ rằng khi thương hiệu còn mới, ông quyết định thuê mặt bằng ngã ba trên phố Lê Đại Hành với mục tiêu không chỉ kinh doanh mà còn quảng bá hình ảnh.
Thời điểm bắt đầu thuê, giá mặt bằng khoảng 200 triệu đồng/tháng. Chủ hệ thống xem vị trí đông người qua lại như một khoản đầu tư cho nhận diện thương hiệu, thay vì chỉ đánh giá hiệu quả dựa trên lợi nhuận tại riêng cửa hàng đó. Vị trí đông người qua lại tại nút giao Lê Đại Hành là kênh quảng bá trực quan, giúp thương hiệu tăng khả năng tiếp cận khách hàng hơn việc chi tiền chạy quảng cáo trực tuyến.
Theo chuyên gia Trần Khánh Minh Sơn, sở hữu mặt bằng đẹp không đồng nghĩa với việc chắc chắn kinh doanh có lãi. Với một cửa hàng phải trả 350 triệu đồng tiền thuê mỗi tháng, doanh thu cần đạt khoảng 1,75-2,33 tỷ đồng/tháng nếu muốn duy trì tỷ lệ chi phí thuê ở mức 15-20% doanh thu.
Đây là mục tiêu không dễ đạt được, bởi ngoài tiền thuê, cửa hàng còn phải chi trả nguyên liệu, nhân sự, điện nước, vận hành và nhiều khoản chi phí khác. Do đó, bài toán lựa chọn mặt bằng không chỉ nằm ở khả năng thu hút khách, mà còn ở việc cân đối chi phí và hiệu quả kinh doanh dài hạn.

articles.title: Biết suy luận lẫn ghi nhớ, vì sao AI có thể không bao giờ thực sự có ý thức?
articles.text:
Một chatbot có thể suy luận, ghi nhớ và thay đổi quan điểm, nhưng điều đó không đồng nghĩa nó sở hữu ý thức. Theo bài viết của nhà nghiên cứu Harvard David Weinberger đăng trên MIT Press Reader, trí tuệ nhân tạo thiếu một yếu tố cốt lõi: cơ thể sống để đánh cược.
Trong bối cảnh các hệ thống trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) ngày càng tinh vi, tranh luận về khả năng máy móc đạt tới ý thức đang trở nên nóng hơn bao giờ hết. Theo quan điểm triết học mang tên thuyết chức năng, ý thức được quyết định bởi những gì một thực thể làm được chứ không phải chất liệu cấu tạo nên nó.
Dựa trên lập luận này, nếu AI đủ sức trò chuyện, suy luận, ghi nhớ, thay đổi quan điểm và thể hiện sự tò mò lẫn cảm xúc, thì việc nó được làm từ máu thịt, silicon hay gạch LEGO đều không quan trọng. Thậm chí, có ý kiến còn cho rằng việc phủ nhận ý thức của một thực thể như vậy sẽ là một dạng định kiến hẹp hòi mới.
Tuy nhiên, bất chấp gợi ý từ lãnh đạo một số công ty AI, tác giả có sách bán chạy kiêm nhà nghiên cứu tại Harvard và cựu giáo sư triết học David Weinberger lại đưa ra góc nhìn hoàn toàn trái ngược.
Trong bài viết trích từ cuốn "Beautiful Particulars" đăng tải trên MIT Press Reader, ông khẳng định các mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn (LLM) mà con người đang trò chuyện cùng không hề có ý thức - không phải vì lý do thực nghiệm, mà bởi bản thân khái niệm đó không có ý nghĩa hợp lý.
Nghịch lý "căn phòng Trung Hoa" và giới hạn của máy tính
Để chứng minh quan điểm của mình, David Weinberger bắt đầu từ thí nghiệm tư tưởng nổi tiếng mang tên "căn phòng Trung Hoa" do triết gia John Searle (1932-2025) đưa ra vào năm 1980. Trong giả định này, một người không hề biết tiếng Trung hay nhận diện được chữ Hán ngồi trong căn phòng kín chỉ có một khe hở, bên cạnh là cuốn sách khổng lồ hướng dẫn bằng tiếng Anh cách đối chiếu các nét vẽ nguệch ngoạc.
Khi một mẩu giấy tiếng Trung được luồn vào, người này chỉ việc tra sách, chép lại các ký hiệu tương ứng rồi đẩy ra ngoài. Người nói tiếng Trung ở bên ngoài sẽ tin chắc họ đang đối thoại với ai đó hiểu ngôn ngữ của mình, dù người bên trong chỉ đang sắp xếp những ký hiệu hoàn toàn vô nghĩa.
Theo Searle, máy tính - kể cả những hệ thống trông như có ý thức - vận hành theo đúng nguyên tắc đó: chúng thao tác trên các ký hiệu mà không hề nhận thức ý nghĩa của chúng. Vì ý nghĩa của ký hiệu phải do một ý thức khác bên ngoài gán vào nên nó chỉ mang tính ngoại tại.
Trái lại, ý thức con người mang tính nội tại. Khi ta bị bỏng tay vào quai nồi nóng, cắn một miếng chuối hay sải bước tản bộ, bộ não nằm trong cơ thể sống trực tiếp cảm nhận nỗi đau, mùi vị và chuyển động mà không cần bất kỳ bước phiên dịch ký hiệu nào.
Sự quan tâm và vai trò không thể thay thế của cơ thể sống
Nếu John Searle dừng lại mà chưa lý giải cội nguồn của tính nội tại, thì nửa thế kỷ trước đó, triết gia Martin Heidegger (1889-1976) đã chạm tới câu trả lời trong kiệt tác "Tồn tại và thời gian" xuất bản năm 1927.
Khảo sát trải nghiệm đời thường của con người, Heidegger nhận thấy mọi sự vật luôn hiện ra dưới lăng kính của dự định hiện tại - chẳng hạn chiếc lọ mứt rỗng có thể trở thành cái cốc khi thiếu ly uống nước, hoặc biến thành chậu hoa tạm thời cho một mục đích khác.
Sở dĩ thế giới có ý nghĩa với con người là vì ta biết dự định và sinh mạng của mình luôn đối mặt với rủi ro, quy về nhận thức rằng một ngày nào đó - thậm chí ngay hôm nay - ta sẽ chết. Mở rộng lập luận của Heidegger, David Weinberger cho rằng vòng lặp giữa rủi ro và sự quan tâm chỉ thực sự có điểm dừng khi gắn với thực tế con người mang trong mình một cơ thể sống.
Cơ thể buộc phải có sự quan tâm mang tính nội tại để né tránh nỗi đau, ăn uống, ngủ nghỉ và tìm kiếm khoái cảm. Cơn đói, cảm giác buồn ngủ, vị ngon của lát bánh táo, cơn đau khi đá trúng ngón chân hay cái ôm từ một đứa trẻ trèo vào lòng cha mẹ đều được cơ thể cảm nhận trực tiếp, hoàn toàn không giống một vết mực xa lạ cần giải mã.
Thế giới cụ thể - ranh giới mà AI không thể chạm tới
Theo phân tích của tác giả, sự quan tâm gắn liền với cơ thể sống luôn mang tính cụ thể rõ rệt trên ba phương diện trong đời sống hằng ngày. Thứ nhất, nó luôn hướng tới đối tượng cụ thể bằng cách thức riêng - từ bạn đời, con cái cho tới đôi tất trong máy sấy, chỗ ngứa sau lưng hay con cá vàng cần cho ăn.
Thứ hai, nó gắn với bối cảnh rõ ràng, như việc để tâm tới đôi tất vì trời lạnh hay lo cho con cá vàng vì sợ lũ trẻ buồn và vì bản thân đã gắn bó. Thứ ba, sự quan tâm nhạy cảm với từng chi tiết nhỏ như ánh nhìn, một cử chỉ khó gọi tên hay dáng vẻ ai đó nghiêng người chăm chú lắng nghe.
Tính cụ thể đó được định hình bởi thế giới nơi mỗi người chào đời - điều Heidegger gọi là "tính bị ném vào đời". Không cần sự đồng thuận, con người được sinh ra vào một nền văn hóa, ngôn ngữ, địa điểm và gia đình nhất định, bởi thực thể có cơ thể không thể tồn tại đồng thời ở nhiều không gian hay thời gian khác nhau.
Hoàn cảnh này tác động sâu sắc tới cả thể xác lẫn tâm trí, như phân tích của triết gia kiêm nhà nữ quyền Iris Marion Young (1949-2006) trong bài tiểu luận năm 1980 mang tên "Ném bóng như một bé gái". Bà chỉ ra cách môi trường nuôi dạy một bé gái tại nơi như nước Mỹ ảnh hưởng ngay cả tới cách các em ôm sách, bước qua đá ngang suối và hình thành tâm lý "tôi không thể" trước nhiều dự định.
Cuối cùng, David Weinberger kết luận rằng con người sở hữu ý thức bởi ta không bị giam hãm trong một căn phòng chỉ biết giải mã những ký hiệu bí ẩn. Khi bước ra thế giới bằng cơ thể sống, cảm giác ướt sũng giữa cơn mưa bão bất chợt là một trải nghiệm trực diện chứ không phải ký hiệu.
Chính sự cởi mở nội tại và trực tiếp với thế giới thông qua thân xác ấy là điều mà AI hoàn toàn không có - và là lý do một chatbot, dù thông minh đến đâu, vẫn chẳng có gì để đánh cược hay mất đi.

articles.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.
The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.
Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”
Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.
In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”
Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?
Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.
Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.
A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”
How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.
A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”
For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.
Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.
“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”
Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.
Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.
Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”
Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

articles.title: 10 things you should never do on your Android phone - Engadget
articles.text:
10 things you should never do on your Android phone
Avoid major mistakes that make your Android phone less secure and less convenient to use.
If you've used Android for a while, you probably know some of its most important rules. But even with an OS that's been around for more than 15 years, myths and outdated assumptions still persist. Or you might be new to Android and not totally sure how to best take care of your device.
Either way, Android doesn't come with a complete user manual, so we've compiled some of the mistakes you shouldn't make on an Android phone. They include ignoring security features and trying advanced functions without understanding them. Follow these, and your Android phone should last years in good condition.
1. Skip software updates
Why it's bad: Software updates fix known vulnerabilities. Patches in a software update are often responsive, meaning they protect against attacks that are happening, not just theoretical threats. Also, if you use high-security apps like banking and wallet tools, those services won't work if your phone gets too behind on security updates.
Who says so: Security vulnerabilities in Android are reported to Google, and Google shares this information confidentially with Android device makers. You can read about what threats Google considers critical on its Android Security page.
Google doesn't share this information publicly for 90 days, giving vendors time to create proper patches and preventing would-be attackers from taking advantage of the details before people have a chance to install patches. There are a lot of players here: Google is responsible for Android software, then every phone maker adds software to Android devices that needs to be patched. Chip makers like MediaTek and Qualcomm also need to patch the drivers that allow those chips to function properly.
What's the best practice: Install every security update as soon as it appears. Also, open the Google Play Store and make sure to update apps regularly — automatic updates are best.
2. Neglect basic Android maintenance
Why it's bad: When your phone is running too many processes at once, it slows down. That seems obvious, but what's actually happening is your phone is shuttling apps between three internal components: storage, RAM and a special partition of RAM called ZRAM made to quickly store and recall active processes.
When your RAM fills up, it starts compressing processes so it can cram them into the ZRAM partition. When there's no more room in ZRAM for compressed data, your phone enters a state called memory thrashing, where it repeatedly loads data from the ZRAM and then compresses it back in an ongoing cycle. This causes your phone to slow down and heat up as the CPU drains power.
Who says so: The Android Open Source Project offers technical details on the so-called "low memory killer daemon" (the software process that stuffs data into ZRAM), and the problems caused when you let that memory fill up with extraneous data pages.
What's the best practice: Restart your phone regularly to clear the RAM and ZRAM. When you're done with a heavy app like a game, swipe to close it from the app switcher menu (though you don't need to do this constantly for all apps). Finally, uninstall apps that you no longer use to make sure they aren't running processes you don't need. On Android, even if you don't open an app, it may still run and use your RAM in the background.
As another part of core maintenance, make sure to keep enough space free on your Android phone. Running it with maxed-out storage means it has no room for temporary caches and other "helper" data.
3. Install apps from untrustworthy sources
Why it's bad: There is no easier way for bad actors to take advantage of security flaws than from apps that come from outside Google's Play Store garden. One common practice is for bad apps to take advantage of your phone's Accessibility controls, which grant privileges for copying your phone's screen and running apps in the background. Google is cautious about approving accessibility access on the Play Store, which is why bad apps are often found on third-party sites.
Who says so: According to Google's security blog, Google Play Protect identified more than 13 million malicious apps from outside the Play Store in 2024 — and those are just the ones the service was able to detect. The standards for Android app security are set by the App Defense Alliance, part of Linux, which forms the foundation of Android's code.
What's the best practice: If you must install apps from outside Google Play, make sure you 100 percent trust the source. A first-party developer you trust, or a security-conscious third-party app market like F-Droid, is better than a random forum or Reddit page. Always use caution outside the Google Play Store.
4. Disable Android's security protections
Why it's bad: If you're asked to disable Google Play Protect for any reason, that's a major red flag. Usually, a scammer will try to convince you to download a phony app by pretending to be your bank or another trusted source. When you try to install the new app, you get a warning from Play Protect, which the scammer tells you to disregard. Never ignore this warning.
Who says so: Play Protect has been a part of Android for almost 10 years, and it gets constant updates that make it more stringent. It's the primary line of defense against dangerous apps you try to install.
What's the best practice: Never disable Google Play Protect, but don't trust it blindly either. Researchers like Bitdefender claim to have found apps that made it to the Play Store and still pose a risk, so you still need to be careful about what you install.
5. Root your phone without a good reason
Why it's bad: In the early days of Android, there were good reasons to obtain root access to your phone. You could enable features that were inexplicably turned off, like network tethering on Verizon's early Android devices. It allows you to remove bloatware installed by your mobile carrier, or even load an OS like CyanogenMod that was better than what Samsung or Google provided. Those days are over.
Rooting a phone triggers failures in Google's Play Integrity API, and that's a break that can't heal. You won't be able to use banking or financial apps or any apps that rely on your phone's Strong integrity, a tag that disappears when you obtain root access to your system. Having root access means mistakes or malicious apps can cause much more damage.
Who says so: Even the US government says this is a bad idea. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) warns against rooting your mobile device, listing rooting and jailbreaking a phone as a threat in its Mobile Threat Catalogue.
What's the best practice: There is not enough reason to root your primary Android phone today if you aren't a software developer. Phone features are no longer restricted based on which carrier sold you the phone. And phone makers let you remove (or at least hide) the bloat — you can even remove Google apps that used to be permanently stuck in your app drawer.
If you have an old device that no longer gets updates, rooting and installing a custom ROM can bring new life to it, but the trade-offs aren't worth it on an in-support daily phone.
6. Use advanced tools that you don't understand
Why it's bad: Say your new Android phone came with a bunch of apps you don't want. The Settings menu lets you disable them so they disappear, but they're still taking up space and you can't let it go.
So, you found a YouTube video that shows you how to turn on USB Debugging, which lets you manage your phone's files from your PC. You figure this isn't a problem, since you aren't installing anything from a third party or handing your phone to a stranger.
Except those instructions often skip an important final step: remember to turn USB Debugging off. Otherwise, your phone is more vulnerable to attacks using a computer. While Android requires you to authorize the connection when you connect to any PC for the first time, you might not realize what you're doing, or someone could trick you into handing over access. That's why it's important to watch the prompts when connecting to an unknown USB port (more on this below).
There are lots of features on Android that can give you advanced access to your system without being dangerous, as long as you're careful to turn them off when you're done.
Who says so: Google is enthusiastic about Android users trying Developer Mode, but admits "it's essential to understand the implications of each setting." That's a massive understatement, since these options can cause problems if you don't know what they do.
What's the best practice: If you dabble in the Android cauldron, be sure to put out the fire. Disable USB Debugging and any other features that you turned on once the task is done. Follow instructions closely, and don't mess with features you don't truly understand.
7. Use public Wi-Fi for sensitive matters
Why it's bad: When you access an open Wi-Fi network, you have no guarantees of privacy. Anyone else who joins the network can use free analyzer tools to see what's happening.
