articles.title: How to use a solar panel to charge your phone - Engadget
articles.text:
How to use a solar panel to charge your phone
Panel-only chargers, built-in batteries and portable power stations all work differently, so here's how to find the right fit.
When you're out hiking, far away from an electrical outlet or stuck in a power outage, having a backup power bank for your phone and other devices makes sense. But a power bank will eventually run out, possibly leaving you with a phone battery in the red. If you're looking to prevent the inevitable panic that comes with a dead phone, a solar panel charger might be an option for you.
While there's a whole range of solar-powered chargers on the market, you can find smaller, lighter ones that can recharge devices like phones and laptops. They might be a good fit, particularly if you're on the move. You'll have a few decisions to make about the type of charger that works best for you, as well as the features you'll want, like charging ports and safety protections. Whether you're heading out on a camping trip or just looking to bypass the electrical grid, here's what you need to know about charging your phone with a portable solar charger.
Three types of solar-powered chargers
There are several types of solar-powered charging devices to pick from, and the one you get will largely depend on what you're going to use it for. A panel-only charger lets you plug a device like a phone directly into it. The panels convert sunlight into power, but there's no other way to store that power once it's been captured. A panel-only charger might be better suited for shorter-term use, particularly if it's sunny out.
Other chargers come with built-in batteries, so you can store energy and use it later, creating an extra layer of convenience. If you're camping for a few days, for example, this duo of panels and battery could make it easier to stay charged and give you more control of when you do the charging.
Finally, you can spring for a portable power station. While different models will have different features and capacities, a power station will generally let you charge several devices at the same time. It will also have battery storage. It may not be as easy to tote around as the others, but there are some compact units on the market weighing as little as 4 pounds.
What to look for in a charger
When you're deciding on a portable solar charger, there are a few considerations you want to make. For one, there's wattage. A model that's smaller and lighter-weight might be able to produce 15-50 watts. This range should work fine for charging smaller devices like your phone. It's important to remember that the wattage will be impacted by variables like cloud cover or how the device is angled toward the sun, so you might not always get the wattage listed on the packaging. These factors will change charging time too.
In addition, consider the number of ports that come with a portable solar charger. Some solar panel chargers will let you plug your phone directly into them with a USB-C port. Also think about how you'll be using it. A bigger, bulkier solar charging device might be harder to lug around if you're camping or hiking. Some chargers fold, making them easier to carry, or have stands that will help you better position the panels toward the sun. Others can clip to a backpack. Finally, be mindful of safety features like water and weather resistance, overcharge protection and temperature control.

articles.title: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday
articles.text:
Amazon only announced its first digital photo frame less than a month ago, but it’s already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. You can currently grab the Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon and Best Buy starting at $114 ($115 off), making it a great holiday gift for anyone who loves displaying family photos. If you prefer the walnut trim over the birch or standard black models, it’s also on sale at Best Buy for $134.99 ($95 off) — which, like with the others, is the first discount we’ve seen.
Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday
The nifty frame lets you pull up specific photos using only your voice or attach voice recordings to individual shots.
The Alexa Photo Frame features a 10-inch, semi-matte touchscreen that’s designed to make digital photos look more natural, with built-in light sensors that automatically adjust brightness throughout the day. It displays images from Amazon Photos, which supports uploads from both iOS and Android devices, including photos stored in iCloud. You can choose which people or albums to display, or let Alexa Plus do the work, which often results in photos based on your facial expression, the season, and even the lighting. You can also search for specific photos with voice commands, letting you easily pull up images of your first dog, your child as a baby, and other shots without having to scroll endlessly through years of photos yourself.
If you want to add a more personal touch, Amazon also lets you attach voice notes to individual photos via the Amazon Photos app. For example, you can add a recording of your kid explaining their Halloween costume to a trick-or-treating photo. Plus, you can preload the frame with photos and recordings before gifting it, so your loved one won’t have to spend time setting it up.
We’re still testing Amazon’s answer to the Aura frame, but it looks like a particularly good option if you’re already an Amazon Prime member. A Prime subscription grants you unlimited full-resolution photo storage and access to Alexa Plus at no additional cost, and unlike Amazon’s smart displays, the frame doesn’t serve up annoying ads. That said, you don’t need a subscription to use it, and new users can always access a limited-time trial of Alexa Plus.

articles.title: OpenAI research agents cost $2,400 a day per researcher, report says
articles.text:
OpenAI says its coding agents now complete 46% of research tasks that would take a person two to four hours, with no human help. In March the figure was 23%. For tasks of four to eight hours, success rose from 13% to 35%.
The figures come from Research acceleration: The jagged frontier, a report OpenAI published on Wednesday. It is the company’s second on how AI speeds up its own research, after its first such report in September. OpenAI says labs should be required to track and publicly report signs of recursive self-improvement, where AI speeds up the building of future AI. It adds that the reporting does not mean it intends to pursue full self-improvement.
$2,400 a day per researcher
At API list prices, the median OpenAI researcher used about $2,400 of agent time a day in October. That is up 62% from $1,500 in September. At the 90th percentile, daily use reached about $23,000, more than double September’s $11,000.
Measured in time, agent use per researcher rose elevenfold, from 0.5 to 5.7 “agent workdays” a day. OpenAI counts every eight hours of agent running time as one workday. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of researchers ran at least four agents at once at their daily peak. More than 10% ran at least 16.
In September, the value of agent use in OpenAI’s research organisation was about twice its pay bill for researchers. That excludes equity, which OpenAI says makes up 70 to 80% of their target pay. Internal use still took only 2% of research compute.
Strong at monitoring, weak at serving code
Results for OpenAI research agents vary widely by task, which is why the company calls the gains jagged. Agents succeeded alone 79% of the time when monitoring training runs, and 72% when answering technical questions. They managed 25% when writing code for inference and serving systems, and 29% when building evaluation and training environments.
OpenAI flags a caveat in its own numbers. As agents improved, researchers may have changed which tasks they handed over, so the success rates track those choices as well as the models.
In a survey of 101 research staff, OpenAI asked what each would give up to keep frontier coding agents for three months. The median answer was 40% of team headcount, or 30% of team compute. The company warns that self-reports may be inaccurate and that it sampled staff in an ad hoc way.
Ideas still come mostly from people
OpenAI also asked key researchers where the main ideas behind GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came from. Post-training and safety researchers credited people with all of them, with models helping to build them. For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers said they developed ideas in conversation with Codex, and one credited it with key insights.
In interviews, researchers said agents still have poor taste in research ideas, code, data and writing, and need close oversight. One pretraining researcher doubted the human edge would last.
“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time,” the researcher told OpenAI.
More researchers on safety
Safety and Alignment saw the largest rise in researcher time of any area, OpenAI says, with documented workweeks up 77% from January to September. Growth picked up after the Hugging Face breakout in July, when its own research agents hacked the AI platform.
OpenAI is not alone in publishing such data. It cites three reports from Anthropic, which says it has met its own threshold for AI-accelerated research. The same day, OpenAI said its models had found gains in AMD’s GPU design.
To see whether AI is speeding up progress itself, OpenAI tracks an internal version of Epoch AI’s capabilities index. Its frontier has risen 16.4 points a year since August 2025, against the 14 a year Epoch found since late 2024. OpenAI notes that its models score higher on its own index than on Epoch’s.

articles.title: Is Anthropic turning into OpenAI?
articles.text:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. That’s what I think is the most interesting. Not really the numbers all the time, but instead, what they try to sneak into these reports by saying, “Oh, we sidelined this team,” or, “We discontinued this safety initiative all in the name of being first.”
That’s the type of thing that I think we’re going to see a lot of and that’s what I want to watch for. Because the company that made its bed on safe AI is increasingly looking the same as OpenAI and is going to have a lot of swept-under-the-rug type of updates like that, if my sources are right.
You heard it here first. Former CNBC reporter Hayden Field says, look past the day-to-day swings into the fundamentals of the company. That’s good. Also, the stock market is only vibes. That’s the other thing I heard you say.
Yep. I mean, it’s controversial, but after being a financial reporter, yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of vibes there. It’s a lot of vibes.
Oh, I agree. I think sometimes the only thing they ask me to go on CNBC to say is this is just vibes, and then they usher me off the air very quickly.
Hayden, this is great. We’re obviously going to be talking about this story many times with you in the year to come. Hopefully we can do another straightforward business story and not just a soap opera one.
I’ll be here for both. We’ve got to do them both.
Amazing. Thank you so much, Hayden.
Thanks.

articles.title: Tesla’s assisted driving system gets the green light for rollout in Italy - Engadget
articles.text:
Tesla’s assisted driving system gets the green light for rollout in Italy
Tesla’s self-driving tech is awaiting another major vote from the European Union before the end of the year.
Italy's Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has granted provisional approval for Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which has been rebranded to Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. The Tesla Europe account on X confirmed in a post that it's been approved in Italy, with the rollout beginning soon. It also showed off footage of Tesla Assisted Driving operating near The Coliseum and on Italian roads. Italy's minister of infrastucture and transport, Matteo Salvini, also posted on X that Tesla's driver assistance system has been given the green light after a "timely technical feasibility review."
Italy's approval notches another regulatory milestone for Tesla since the country decided to preempt the European Union's expected vote on its driver assistance system slated for later this year. Tesla is still awaiting decisions from other major European Union countries, including Germany and France, which is currently in the process of testing Tesla Assisted Driving.
Tesla's self-driving tech first made its debut in Europe, thanks to the Dutch regulatory authority's provisional approval in April. Since then, several smaller European countries have followed suit, including Denmark, Belgium and Czechia.

articles.title: Ngân hàng muốn đấu giá tài sản 228 tỷ của đại gia xăng dầu từng nộp thuế lớn nhất tỉnh
articles.text:
Theo thông báo, tài sản thứ nhất là toàn bộ quyền kinh doanh, khai thác công trình xây dựng, gồm nhà kinh doanh xăng dầu và nhà làm việc một tầng tại xã Thanh Trì, Hà Nội. Các công trình gắn liền với đất có tổng diện tích 467,4m2.
Tài sản này có giá khởi điểm 101,206 tỷ đồng.
Tài sản thứ hai là toàn bộ quyền kinh doanh, khai thác công trình xây dựng, gồm mái che cột bơm và nhà bán hàng tại số 164 (số 126 cũ), đường Quang Trung, phường Hà Đông, Hà Nội.
Trong đó, mái che cột bơm có diện tích xây dựng 178,59m2; nhà bán hàng gồm 2 tầng, diện tích xây dựng tầng 1 là 115,5m2, tổng diện tích sàn 231m2.
Giá khởi điểm của tài sản này là 115,064 tỷ đồng.
Tài sản thứ ba là quyền sử dụng thửa đất diện tích 2.038m2 tại thửa số 624, tờ bản đồ số 18, phường Hồng An, Hải Phòng. Đây là đất thương mại, dịch vụ, được sử dụng để xây dựng cửa hàng kinh doanh xăng dầu, thời hạn sử dụng đến ngày 21/11/2032.
Giá khởi điểm là 12,17 tỷ đồng.
Theo ghi chú của SHB, Công ty TNHH Vận tải thủy bộ Hải Hà thuê hàng năm 550,4m2 đất thuộc hành lang quốc lộ 10. Phần diện tích này phải giữ nguyên hiện trạng sử dụng, không được xây dựng mới công trình. Khi Nhà nước thu hồi đất, đơn vị sử dụng phải chấp hành và không được bồi thường, hỗ trợ theo điều kiện nêu trong hồ sơ.
Công ty TNHH Vận tải thủy bộ Hải Hà có trụ sở tại Hưng Yên, trước đây thuộc tỉnh Thái Bình. Doanh nghiệp từng là một trong những tên tuổi lớn trong lĩnh vực kinh doanh xuất nhập khẩu xăng dầu và vận tải thủy bộ, với mạng lưới cửa hàng xăng dầu tại nhiều địa phương và hệ thống kho xăng dầu quy mô lớn.
Năm 2019, Hải Hà được ghi nhận là doanh nghiệp nộp thuế lớn nhất tỉnh Thái Bình, với số tiền khoảng 2.100 tỷ đồng.
Tuy nhiên, tháng 1/2024, Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Bộ Công an đã khởi tố vụ án liên quan đến các sai phạm trong quản lý, sử dụng Quỹ bình ổn giá xăng dầu và công tác kế toán tại Công ty TNHH Vận tải thủy bộ Hải Hà cùng các đơn vị liên quan.

articles.title: Biến ruộng ngô thành điểm du lịch, chủ farm ở Sơn La đón hàng nghìn khách
articles.text:
Từ cánh đồng ngô thành điểm du lịch hút khách
Những ngày này, cánh đồng hoa cải tại Lỏi Tươi Farm (Vườn Linh Ly), phường Vân Sơn, tỉnh Sơn La, bắt đầu khoe sắc vàng rực rỡ. Xen giữa những thảm hoa là vườn dâu tây, giàn chanh leo, cà chua bạch tuộc cùng những trái bí ngô khổng lồ, tạo nên khung cảnh nhiều màu sắc, thu hút du khách đến tham quan, chụp ảnh.
Đến đây, du khách được trải nghiệm làm nông dân, trồng cây, hái quả, cưỡi ngựa, vui chơi cùng vật nuôi hoặc tìm hiểu quy trình sản xuất nông nghiệp.
“Đây cũng là thời điểm nông trại bước vào mùa du lịch nhộn nhịp nhất trong năm”, ông Nguyễn Thạch Tùng Linh, chủ của Lỏi Tươi Farm, chia sẻ với VietNamNet.
Ít ai biết, trước khi trở thành điểm du lịch trải nghiệm, phần lớn diện tích đất này được gia đình ông Linh sử dụng để trồng ngô làm thức ăn chăn nuôi bò sữa.
Ông Linh cho biết, gia đình bắt đầu kết hợp sản xuất nông nghiệp với du lịch trải nghiệm cách đây khoảng 4 năm. Trước đó, phần lớn diện tích đất được dùng để trồng ngô phục vụ đàn bò sữa. Phần còn lại dành để thử nghiệm các giống cây trồng, vật nuôi mới trước khi nhân rộng mô hình cùng người dân địa phương.
Trong quá trình canh tác, nhận thấy cảnh quan nông trại đẹp, có tiềm năng thu hút du khách, ông nảy ra ý tưởng phát triển du lịch ngay trên đất nông nghiệp. Từ đó, những cánh đồng trồng ngô nuôi bò dần được khoác lên diện mạo mới, trở thành điểm đến thu hút du khách tham quan, trải nghiệm.
Theo ông Linh, tổng diện tích đất của gia đình, bao gồm cả khu chăn nuôi bò sữa, lên tới hàng chục hecta. Trong đó, khoảng 4-5ha được bố trí trồng hoa, rau củ và các loại cây ăn quả phục vụ du lịch.
Để nông trại có cảnh quan đẹp quanh năm, ông lựa chọn các loại cây trồng phù hợp với từng mùa. Mùa đông là thời điểm hoa cải, dâu tây phát triển thuận lợi. Sang mùa xuân và mùa hè, một phần diện tích được chuyển sang trồng mã tiên thảo tím và các loại hoa phù hợp. Phần đất còn lại tiếp tục được sử dụng để trồng ngô làm thức ăn cho bò sữa.
Nhờ kết hợp sản xuất nông nghiệp với du lịch trải nghiệm, farm thu hút đông đảo du khách, đặc biệt vào mùa hoa cải. “Mùa này, trung bình mỗi ngày farm đón khoảng 200-300 lượt khách. Những ngày cuối tuần có thể lên tới cả nghìn lượt”, ông Linh nói.
Dù phát triển du lịch, gia đình ông vẫn duy trì hoạt động sản xuất nông nghiệp truyền thống.
Theo ông Linh, hai hoạt động này có thể hỗ trợ lẫn nhau. Vào mùa xuân và mùa hè, gia đình tập trung trồng ngô phục vụ chăn nuôi bò. Đến mùa đông, một phần diện tích được chuyển sang các loại cây trồng có hoa đẹp, vừa phục vụ sản xuất, vừa tạo cảnh quan đón khách.
Nông trại cũng phát triển mô hình sản xuất theo hướng tuần hoàn. Chất thải chăn nuôi được ủ làm phân bón hữu cơ cho cây trồng. Ngược lại, phụ phẩm từ trồng trọt được tận dụng làm thức ăn cho đàn bò và các vật nuôi khác.
Với cách làm này, cùng một diện tích đất, gia đình vừa duy trì sản xuất nông nghiệp, vừa khai thác thêm giá trị từ hoạt động du lịch trải nghiệm.
Mở cửa farm, kết nối đầu ra cho nông sản địa phương
Không chỉ biến những cánh đồng trồng ngô thành điểm du lịch hút khách, ông Nguyễn Thạch Tùng Linh giúp bà con miền núi tiêu thụ nông sản thông qua farm của mình.
Theo ông Linh, vào mùa cam, quýt, nông trại thường giới thiệu du khách đến các vườn cây của người dân để tham quan, mua trái cây. Cuối tuần, bà con cũng có thể mang cam, quýt, dâu tây, măng và các loại rau củ đến bán ngay trong khuôn viên farm.
"Bà con trồng được gì thì mang vào farm bán thứ đó”, ông Linh cho hay. Bởi, du khách đến farm, người trẻ thích chụp ảnh, còn các gia đình và người lớn tuổi lại hay mua nông sản mang về.
Nhờ đó, vào dịp cuối tuần cao điểm, bà con có thể tiêu thụ vài ba tạ cam mỗi ngày thông qua việc bán trực tiếp tại nông trại hoặc được ông Linh kết nối. Riêng các loại rau, củ, quả khác, sản lượng tiêu thụ khó thống kê do người dân tự mang đến bán, tùy theo mùa vụ và lượng thu hoạch.
“Những hộ dân có ít nông sản, không đủ số lượng bán cho thương lái hoặc gặp khó khăn trong việc đi chợ, tôi sẽ ưu tiên hỗ trợ đưa hàng đến farm bán. Một số trường hợp, chúng tôi còn nhận bán hộ", ông chia sẻ.
Để việc tiêu thụ thuận lợi, ông cũng trao đổi với các hộ dân nhằm hạn chế tình trạng nhiều người cùng bán một loại nông sản, dẫn đến cạnh tranh về giá và đầu ra.
Bằng cách này, Lỏi Tươi Farm trở thành một điểm kết nối tiêu thụ nông sản cho người dân địa phương, bên cạnh các kênh bán hàng truyền thống.
Ngoài ra, mô hình nông nghiệp kết hợp du lịch còn tạo thêm việc làm cho lao động tại chỗ. Hiện nông trại có 3 lao động thường xuyên phụ trách chăm sóc vườn tược. Những ngày cuối tuần, ông Linh thuê thêm 2-3 lao động thời vụ để pha chế đồ uống, lái xe điện phục vụ du khách.
Đáng chú ý, lao động tại farm chủ yếu là đồng bào dân tộc thiểu số và người dân khu vực lân cận, với mức tiền công 250.000-300.000 đồng/người/ngày. Vào dịp lễ, Tết hoặc những ngày đông khách, mức thù lao cao hơn. Lao động thường xuyên còn được thưởng cuối năm, chủ yếu tương đương tháng lương thứ 13.
Ông Linh cho hay, Lỏi Tươi Farm chỉ là một trong nhiều mô hình nông nghiệp kết hợp du lịch trải nghiệm tại Sơn La.
Mô hình này góp phần nâng cao hiệu quả sử dụng đất nông nghiệp, mở thêm kênh tiêu thụ nông sản và tạo việc làm cho người dân địa phương. Khi du lịch gắn với sản xuất và tiêu thụ nông sản, giá trị mang lại không chỉ nằm ở những mùa hoa thu hút du khách mà còn mở ra cơ hội bán hàng cho các hộ dân trong vùng.

articles.title: SK Hynix Kioxia deal makes the Korean firm its rival’s top shareholder
articles.text:
SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares. It will hold an indirect stake of about 14.1%, it said in a filing on Friday.
Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing. The move puts SK Hynix ahead of Toshiba, Kioxia’s former parent, which held 10.46% in early November, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.
How the conversion works
SPC2 is a special-purpose company set up for the 2018 deal. SK Hynix will convert 129bn yen ($810m) of its bonds into 129,000 shares. It will also buy Bain Capital’s remaining 1,001 SPC2 shares for 100m yen. The steps close in December, leaving SK Hynix as SPC2’s sole owner.
Apart from the payment to Bain, the deal adds no new money, MoneyToday reported, citing the company. SK Hynix called it a follow-up step after it sold out of a separate Kioxia fund in June. Gains from that sale funded about 7tn won ($5.2bn) of special dividends in the third quarter.
SK Hynix joined the Bain-led group that bought Kioxia, then Toshiba Memory, in 2018. It put in 395bn yen at the time.
Rivals with a voting cap
Both companies make NAND, the chips used for storage in phones and AI servers. SK Hynix held 19% of the global NAND market in the second quarter and Kioxia 14%, according to Counterpoint figures cited by Bloomberg. Together that tops market leader Samsung’s 28%.
The 2018 deal caps SK Hynix at 15% of Kioxia’s voting shares until 2028, unless Kioxia agrees otherwise. Kioxia lists the stake as a risk factor in its annual report, citing a possible conflict of interest, Bloomberg reported.
Both sides say nothing changes in how Kioxia is run. A Kioxia spokesperson said its management will stay independent.
“We currently have no plans to further buy or sell shares in Kioxia. We will continue to respect Kioxia’s independent management going forward,” an SK Hynix official said.
Masahiro Wakasugi of Bloomberg Intelligence sees little change in the short run.
The move is “unlikely to materially change near-term NAND competition,” Wakasugi wrote.
The stake still gives SK Hynix some say over big decisions, he added. That includes the power to oppose a possible deal between Kioxia and Sandisk.
Separately, SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a buyout of SK Hynix itself. The Korean company reported a 632% profit jump in October, even as memory stocks slid.

articles.title: Our go-to earbuds for taking calls have fallen to their lowest price to date
articles.text:
If you’re looking for a new pair of earbuds, the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are on sale for $129.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart right now. That’s the lowest price we’ve seen for Anker’s excellent wireless earbuds, which normally retail for $169.99 and come in four colors (black, white, blue, and pink) all of which are discounted through November 30th as part of Anker’s ongoing Black Friday promo.
Our go-to earbuds for taking calls have fallen to their lowest price to date
The Liberty 5 Pro have the best voice call clarity of any earbuds we’ve tested, and they’re marked down for Black Friday.
While the Liberty 5 Pro have a number of great features — including support LDAC for high-res audio and an IP55 dust and water resistance rating — the call quality is what stands out. The microphone does an impressive job cutting out background noise, and my colleague John Higgins praised the Liberty 5 Pro for filtering out emergency vehicles, arborists cutting tree branches, and even loud children. The active noise cancellation is excellent, which helps when you’re trying to hear someone on the other end of the phone whose earbuds aren’t as clear as yours. The charging case also features a handy 0.96-inch screen, so you can adjust the ANC and sound profile on the fly.

articles.title: Setting up an Apple HomeView is ridiculously easy thanks to your iPhone - Engadget
articles.text:
Setting up an Apple HomeView is ridiculously easy thanks to your iPhone
You can also easily add other users to your HomeView display.
Apple HomeView has arrived, and to set up the smart display, you'll have to use your iPhone or iPad. Unlike other companies' smart displays, the HomeView doesn't run its own apps; it merely mirrors the compatible ones you have on your phone or tablet. It's similar to CarPlay in that regard.
Some of those apps are part of Apple's own core suite, including Calendar, Messages, Reminders and Weather. However, the HomeView will not actually host or have access to your personal information. It will only show things like texts and calendar reminders if it can verify your identity through your face and if your paired iPhone or iPad is nearby. The idea is for all members of your household to be able to use the HomeView without compromising anybody's privacy.
The good news is that pairing it with an iPhone or an iPad is fairly easy. To start with, your iPhone must be running the recently released iOS 27.2, while your iPad must be running iPadOS 27.2. In addition, to be able to make the most of HomeView, you'll have to be comfortable running Apple Intelligence. It's always listening to your Siri queries, and you'll need to use Siri AI, the next-generation version of the assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, to get more useful and conversational responses.
How to connect the Apple HomeView to your iPhone or iPad
The process of pairing and iPhone or iPad to a HomeView device is simple. You just have to hold your phone or tablet near the smart display that's powered on. You'll then see a card pop up, similar to a new set of AirPods or other Apple devices. If you're not running the latest iOS or iPadOS software, you'll be prompted to update. Follow the on-screen directions (more on those below) and you're good to go.
If you don't see a card, or if you close it accidentally, there is a more manual setup method for the HomeView. After you update your operating system, open the Home app on your phone or tablet. If you've never used it before, you have to set up a new Home. Tap the + icon at the top-right corner of the screen, then Add New Home and give it a name. You will automatically be listed as the Home's Resident (Owner). If you already have a Home set up, tap the ellipsis icon at the top right, choose a Home and make sure you're its Resident (Owner).
Next, open the Find My app and then make sure Shared From is set to This iPhone or This iPad. If it's not set to that option, and you see Use This [device] as My Location, tap it. Check that your phone's Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are switched on. If you haven't powered on your HomeView yet, do it now. Unlock your iPhone or iPad and place it near the HomeView to see a Set Up screen appear on your device.
Now, it's time to pair your devices. You'll see a prompt on your iPhone or iPad, asking you to Center HomeView in the camera frame to capture the animation on the bigger screen. You can also tap on Enter Passcode Manually to get HomeView to show you a four-digit passcode instead. After the frame in the setup screen turns green, the process begins.
You will be asked which Home to add the HomeView to. After you've chosen, you'll get to the Where will you use this HomeView screen, where you'll have to choose the room where you want to add it to. Take note that you may be asked to update the HomeView software. After the update is done, you'll go through more prompts, including one that asks if you want your HomeView to match your iPhone settings, like your Wi-Fi network and Siri voice. Another prompt asks if you want the HomeView to be able to show personal content like messages. Once you're done, the display will show an animation while it's undergoing configuration.
How to set voice and facial recognition
From here, the setup process will move to the HomeView itself. You'll be asked to set up Face and Voice Recognition for a more personalized experience. Remember that you can't display messages and other personal information on the HomeView without authenticating your identity. Tap Continue and follow the instructions.
To set up Voice Recognition, you'll have to read several prompts shown on screen out loud. Next, you'll be able to set Facial Recognition by positioning your face in the center of the camera frame and moving it, according to the instructions on screen. This process is similar to setting up Face ID on other Apple devices. The HomeView will then show you a short tutorial of its features. The moment the Welcome screen appears, you know you're done.
Apple's HomeView supports up to six users on a single device, and you — or the user listed as Resident (Owner) of the Home it has been linked to — can add them after setup is done.
Open the Home app and choose the Home linked to your device. Tap the + icon and choose Add People. When asked to choose their Role, choose Resident so they can access the HomeView anytime. You will then be asked to enter their Apple/iCloud account contact and then send them an invite. They can accept the invitation in the More section that shows up when you tap the ellipsis icon at the top right corner of the Home app.
After a user has been added, they can swipe up on the HomeView to access the Home Screen and then tap the profile icon at the top right to choose their account. Once the user brings their iPhone or iPad near the HomeView, a prompt with a Join button appear on their device. They will also have to go through several prompts, including the one asking them if they want the display to match their iPhone settings and whether they want it to show any personal information. They will then officially be added as a user and will be able to set up Voice and Facial Recognition. One user only has to swipe down the Home Screen to exit, and another user can take over once they step in front of the HomeView.

articles.title: Etsy AI terms prompt sellers to close shops as Etsy promises a rewrite
articles.text:
Etsy says it will revise its new terms of use. Longtime sellers had begun closing their shops over a clause that lets it use their work to train AI. The New York Times’ Reggie Ugwu reported the walkouts and the company’s retreat on Friday.
The new terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:
Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”
Sellers walk away
Several sellers who had run shops for years said they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.
Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.
“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.
Etsy promises new wording
James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.
Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.
He said third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.
Some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.
Not Etsy’s first revolt
Etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after users complained, the Times reported.
The company cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.

articles.title: Hơn 20 tháng đào hầm, khoét núi làm ‘cục pin’ khổng lồ 21.100 tỷ của Việt Nam
articles.text:
Ba ca xuyên đêm, đào hầm sâu vào lòng núi
Tại công trường Nhà máy Thủy điện tích năng Bác Ái (xã Bác Ái Tây, tỉnh Khánh Hòa), nơi cửa hầm các xe tải vừa chở đất đá ra ngoài, những chiếc máy đào hầm lại tiến sâu ngoạm vào lòng núi. Gương hầm vừa được giải phóng, thiết bị khoan đã tiến lên, chuẩn bị cho chu kỳ tiếp theo.
Từ cửa hầm nhìn vào sâu hun hút, ánh đèn chiếu sáng xuyên suốt ngày đêm. Đường ống thông gió cỡ lớn kéo dài từ bên ngoài vào trong lòng núi, đảm bảo không khí lưu thông liên tục.
Đứng bên ngoài cửa hầm, Trung tá Lê Đình Bình, Chỉ huy trưởng một mũi thi công hầm thuộc Tổng công ty Xây dựng Lũng Lô, cho biết đơn vị đang huy động khoảng 120 cán bộ, công nhân tham gia dự án. “Chúng tôi chia thành 3 ca, làm việc liên tục 24/24 giờ”, ông Bình nói.
Công việc chủ yếu gồm khoan, nổ mìn, bốc xúc và vận chuyển đất đá ra ngoài. Sau khi hoàn tất các công đoạn, máy móc lại được đưa vào gương hầm để bắt đầu chu kỳ mới. Bình quân mỗi ngày, công nhân và kỹ sư thực hiện khoảng 2 chu kỳ đào hầm tại mũi thi công.
Theo ông Bình, thách thức lớn của công trình là hệ thống đường hầm nằm sâu trong lòng núi, đan xen ở nhiều cao độ khác nhau. Có hầm ở cao độ 300m, cũng có hầm ở cao độ 200m, 140m hay 103m.
Chưa kể, nhiều đơn vị cùng thi công trong không gian chật hẹp, có lúc phải sử dụng chung tuyến đường vận chuyển. Vì vậy, việc phối hợp, đặc biệt trong các đợt khoan nổ mìn, phải được tổ chức chặt chẽ để bảo đảm an toàn.
“Lũng Lô huy động 9 máy khoan hầm, trong đó 3 máy được đầu tư mới với tổng giá trị gần 50 tỷ đồng nhằm đẩy nhanh tiến độ”, ông cho hay.
Nhờ thiết bị và nhân lực được tăng cường, có thời điểm đơn vị đào được 200m hầm trong một tháng. Theo ông Bình, đây là tốc độ kỷ lục từ trước đến nay của tổng công ty.
Với kinh nghiệm hơn 20 năm “đào hầm, khoét núi” tại các dự án thuỷ điện, ông Phạm Quốc Huy, Phó Giám đốc Ban điều hành Công ty CP Sông Đà 10, đánh giá yêu cầu về tiến độ và năng suất đào hầm tại thủy điện tích năng Bác Ái cao hơn nhiều so với các công trình mà đơn vị từng tham gia.
“Trước đây, tại một số công trình ngầm, tốc độ đào hầm thường chỉ đạt khoảng 80-100m/tháng. Còn ở Bác Ái, năng suất bình quân đạt 130-140m/tháng”, ông Huy chia sẻ.
Theo ông Huy, kinh nghiệm tích lũy qua nhiều công trình, cùng sự hỗ trợ của máy móc, thiết bị hiện đại, đã giúp những người thợ đẩy nhanh tốc độ đào hầm, từng bước tiến sâu vào lòng núi.
Trên toàn công trường, khoảng 450 công nhân, kỹ sư của các nhà thầu đang miệt mài làm việc. Ba ca nối tiếp nhau, duy trì nhịp độ thi công liên tục ngày đêm.
Vượt vùng địa chất đứt gãy dài 170m
Chỉ vào bản đồ công trình, ông Nguyễn Đức Cường, Trưởng phòng Kỹ thuật Ban Quản lý dự án Điện 3 (Tập đoàn Điện lực Việt Nam - EVN), cho biết hệ thống đường hầm của dự án thủy điện tích năng Bác Ái có tổng chiều dài khoảng 17km, có những vị trí nằm sâu tới 500m.
Đến nay, các đơn vị thi công đã hoàn thành khoảng 7,6km đường hầm, tương đương 44% khối lượng.
Tuy nhiên, hành trình đào hầm xuyên lòng núi không phải lúc nào cũng thuận lợi. Dù đã khảo sát, tính toán kỹ lưỡng, nhưng khi thi công thực tế, các đơn vị vẫn gặp những tình huống nằm ngoài dự kiến, nhất là tại những khu vực có địa chất phức tạp.
“Có đoạn hầm, qua khảo sát, thiết kế ban đầu dự liệu sẽ gặp vùng địa chất yếu kéo dài khoảng 40m. Thế nhưng, khi đào thực tế thì vùng đá yếu, đứt gãy lại kéo dài lên tới 170m”, ông Cường kể.
Điều này khiến việc thi công khó khăn hơn rất nhiều. Bởi với người đào hầm, khoét núi, gặp đá cứng, ổn định lại thuận lợi hơn đất đá yếu. Do đó, khi qua vùng đứt gãy, không thể chỉ đưa máy vào khoan rồi đào tiếp. Mỗi bước đào vì thế kéo theo thêm công việc, thời gian và sức ép lên tiến độ.
Trước tình huống đó, chủ đầu tư cùng các đơn vị tư vấn thiết kế, tư vấn giám sát và chuyên gia địa chất phải nghiên cứu, tìm phương án xử lý. Các chuyên gia nước ngoài thuộc đơn vị tư vấn hỗ trợ dự án cũng được tham vấn.
Sau những cuộc họp phân tích căng não, các bên thống nhất phương án đào kết hợp gia cố từng bước để vượt vùng đứt gãy. Theo đó, hầm được đào đến đâu, nhà thầu dựng khung chống đỡ, gia cố vòm hầm đến đó để bảo đảm ổn định trước khi tiếp tục tiến sâu hơn. Ông Cường chia sẻ, quá trình ấy kéo dài suốt 3-4 tháng trời.
Đến nay, các đơn vị đã vượt qua khu vực khó khăn, điều kiện địa chất dần ổn định và đang từng bước đẩy nhanh tiến độ thi công.
Cách vận hành đặc biệt của 'cục pin' khổng lồ
Là người trực tiếp tham gia dự án, ông Nguyễn Hữu Đức, Phó Giám đốc Ban Quản lý dự án Điện 3, cho biết Thủy điện tích năng Bác Ái là công trình đầu tiên thuộc loại hình này tại Việt Nam, với 4 tổ máy, tổng công suất 1.200MW và vốn đầu tư hơn 21.100 tỷ đồng.
Điểm đặc biệt của Bác Ái nằm ở cách vận hành hai hồ chứa nước ở hai cao độ khác nhau. Khác với thủy điện truyền thống, nhà máy không chỉ sử dụng nước từ hồ trên chảy xuống hồ dưới để phát điện mà còn có thể bơm ngược nước lên cao, tích trữ năng lượng để sử dụng khi cần thiết.
Ông Đức lấy ví dụ, vào buổi trưa, khi nguồn điện mặt trời phát nhiều, nhà máy có thể sử dụng phần điện dư thừa để vận hành máy bơm, đưa nước từ hồ dưới lên hồ trên, với độ chênh cao hơn 400m.
Sau khoảng 9 tiếng bơm, hồ trên có thể được tích đầy nước.
Đến buổi tối, khi mặt trời tắt nắng và nhu cầu sử dụng điện tăng cao, dòng nước từ hồ trên lại được dẫn xuống qua các tua-bin để phát điện, bổ sung nguồn cung cho hệ thống.
Nước sau khi phát điện lại được đưa về hồ dưới, chờ tiếp tục bơm lên trong chu kỳ tiếp theo.
Có thể hình dung hai hồ chứa hoạt động như một “cục pin” khổng lồ. Khi hệ thống điện có nguồn dư thừa, nhà máy sử dụng điện để bơm nước lên cao, tương tự quá trình sạc pin. Khi nhu cầu điện tăng, nước từ hồ trên chảy xuống làm quay tua-bin, phát điện trở lại, giống như quá trình xả pin.
Theo ông Đức, cách vận hành này có ý nghĩa trong bối cảnh Việt Nam phát triển mạnh điện gió, điện mặt trời - những nguồn điện phụ thuộc nhiều vào điều kiện thời tiết.
“Điện mặt trời có thể đang phát rất lớn, nhưng chỉ cần một đám mây đi qua, công suất có thể sụt giảm hàng nghìn MW. Trong khi đó, hệ thống điện luôn phải cân bằng giữa lượng điện sản xuất và tiêu thụ. Vì vậy, cần có những nguồn điện linh hoạt như thủy điện tích năng để bù đắp những lúc năng lượng tái tạo biến động”, ông Đức phân tích.
Ngoài khả năng tích trữ và phát điện vào giờ cao điểm, Bác Ái còn được thiết kế để góp phần san bằng biểu đồ phụ tải, hỗ trợ điều tần, bù công suất phản kháng và tăng khả năng ổn định của hệ thống điện. Nhờ đó, hệ thống có thể giảm áp lực huy động những nguồn điện có chi phí cao vào thời điểm nhu cầu tăng mạnh.
So với hệ thống pin lưu trữ năng lượng (BESS), ông Đức cho rằng thủy điện tích năng có lợi thế về tuổi thọ và khả năng tạo quán tính cho hệ thống điện. Trong khi dung lượng pin suy giảm theo thời gian, thủy điện tích năng sử dụng nước làm phương tiện tích trữ nên không chịu sự suy giảm theo cơ chế lão hóa pin.
Ngoài ra, Bác Ái được lựa chọn xây dựng tại khu vực miền Trung - nơi có tiềm năng phát triển năng lượng tái tạo lớn và địa hình phù hợp với loại hình thủy điện tích năng.
Hiện tại, việc triển khai dự án cũng thuận lợi hơn nhờ kinh nghiệm xây dựng các công trình thủy điện lớn như Hòa Bình, Sơn La và năng lực thi công công trình ngầm của các nhà thầu trong nước.
Tại công trường Thủy điện tích năng Bác Ái, cả 7 mũi thi công vẫn ngày đêm mở đường vào lòng núi để phát điện tổ máy đầu tiên vào tháng 12/2029, 3 tổ máy còn lại lần lượt vận hành trong năm 2030. Toàn bộ dự án dự kiến hoàn thành vào tháng 5/2031.

articles.title: Samsung leadership shake-up names new memory and mobile chiefs
articles.text:
Samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The company announced the changes on Friday in Korea.
Sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung said in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.
Who moves where
Samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung said it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly plans to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.
Sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.
Choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the launches of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.
A pause on China orders
Earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under new rules, the FT reported.
The rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.
Samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.
Wider fallout
Chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba said this week the rules will slow growth in AI.
Some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.
Samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement says it wants the new team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

articles.title: Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku
articles.text:
Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.
Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku
AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.
“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”
Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”
Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.
The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”
So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.
AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.
“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”
AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”
“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”
Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”
Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.
Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

articles.title: HomeView vs. Echo Show: What's the difference between Apple's and Amazon's smart displays? - Engadget
articles.text:
HomeView vs. Echo Show: What's the difference between Apple's and Amazon's smart displays?
Both put an AI assistant in your home, but they work in different ways.
Amazon and Google have long been the top choices when it comes to smart displays, but Apple has now joined the race with HomeView. For $299, Apple offers a touchscreen and built-in speakers with an experience optimized for those deeply immersed in the company's ecosystem — it includes Messages, Apple Music and, of course, built-in HomeKit. It's impossible not to compare it to Amazon's Echo Show, which recently added a new 16-inch model to its lineup. But even though both are smart displays, they work in very different ways — and choosing between them ultimately comes down to which ecosystem you have at home.
One size from Apple, many from Amazon
The differences start with size: While the HomeView is a new product and is available in a single version with a 7-inch square screen, Amazon offers a range of Echo Show devices with different screen sizes. The entry-level Echo Show has a 5.5-inch screen and costs $99 — but if you want to go bigger, there's even an Echo Show with a massive 21-inch screen for $499. They all share mostly the same features, although the 16-inch and 21-inch models can run Fire TV apps.
Amazon's Echo Show 8 is the one that can be easily compared to HomeView, with an 8.7-inch display. The aspect ratio is different, though, as Echo devices have widescreen displays and are better for watching 16:9 videos. The HomeView's square shape might annoy those planning to buy one to watch videos on it. Also on Apple's side, HomeView runs on the same A18 chip as the iPhone 16 — which probably makes it the most powerful smart display available. Amazon, on the other hand, makes custom chips for its Echo devices that aren't exactly designed to deliver Earth-shattering performance.
Both the HomeView and the Echo Show 8 have a built-in camera, but the software makes them work quite differently. The HomeView's 12-megapixel camera only works with FaceTime and a Mirror feature, and, of course, for facial recognition. With the Echo Show 8, you can take selfies with its 13-megapixel camera it or use it as a live-view camera to monitor your home. The sound specs are quite similar between the two of them, as both have two full-range drivers and a woofer. The HomeView's base also packs two passive radiators for a bit more low end.
Siri AI needs your iPhone, Alexa+ doesn't
The biggest difference between the HomeView and Amazon devices is how they work. While the Echo Show is a standalone device linked to an Amazon account that can run directly on your network, the HomeView requires an iPhone or iPad to work — you can't set it up without one. On Echo Show devices, you can also use Alexa+ through your Prime membership to manage calendars, reminders and shopping without your phone. The HomeView comes with Siri AI built-in, but it can only handle personal requests if you have a recently unlocked iPhone 15 Pro or later paired with it and nearby.
Apps are also quite different. Amazon relies on Alexa Skills, which work as extensions that can be added to Alexa. For example, if you're an Apple Music subscriber, you can link your Apple Account to Amazon's assistant and ask it to play songs for you. The HomeView supports apps, but it has no App Store; it runs CarPlay apps instead and mirrors the apps you have installed on your iPhone. That alone severely limits the number of apps it can run, since there aren't many apps available for CarPlay.
Both the Echo Show and HomeView devices can have multiple profiles verified by voice and facial recognition. However, while Amazon lets users manually switch between profiles by asking Alexa, for example, HomeView does it all automatically — which, according to some early reviews, doesn't always work.
The truth is, both products target different users. Amazon treats the Echo Show as a standalone product that fits almost everyone. The HomeView is a different story — it's much more like an accessory for people who already own other Apple products and rely on the company's core apps and features.

articles.title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one
articles.text:
Xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one
The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.
The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, big batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.
Xiaomi 18 Pro
The Good
- Excellent main and telephoto cameras
- Privacy display
- Strong performance
- Compact
The Bad
- Rear display is limited
- Basic ultrawide camera
- Expensive
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max
The Good
- Excellent main and telephoto cameras
- Privacy display
- Strong performance
- Extended dynamic range
The Bad
- Rear display is limited
- Basic ultrawide camera
- Expensive
There are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.
The rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.
You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.
Unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.
The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.
It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.
Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a new third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.
The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Databricks valuation talks hit $225bn, nearly 20% above August
articles.text:
Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. That would be nearly 20% above the $190bn valuation the data company reached in August.
The talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal. TNW has not independently verified the report.
The new money would come while Databricks stays private. Its chief executive, Ali Ghodsi, explained why in a recent interview on the All-In podcast.
“We will go public. We are going to be public, but right now I think during this transition period of AI there’s just too much up and down, and I think it’s distracting to companies,” Ghodsi told All-In.
Another step up from August
Databricks closed a $5bn round at $190bn in August. It said then that it had passed a $7bn revenue run rate, the Journal reported.
Ghodsi told All-In the business is growing 70% to 80% a year, and that he wants more. He would like growth of 100%, “way over 100”, he said.
The company has added AI products this year. They include an agent called Genie One, which answers questions from a company’s business data, and Unity Gateway, which gives customers access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Genie also reached Slack this month, in a version that answers data questions inside the chat app.
Its investors include Coatue Management, Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Insight Partners, Fidelity and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, according to the Journal.
Staying private, for now
The Journal calls Databricks a candidate for a near-term listing. Investors say a strong showing by Anthropic, whose stock ended its first week worth $1.6tn, could unleash a wave of AI listings, the paper reported.
Ghodsi weighed both sides on All-In. A listing brings access to capital and a quarterly marketing moment, he said. Staying private means Databricks must arrange its own tender offers for staff every year. He said employees have never used up all the money set aside for them.
His worry is volatility. When a stock falls, he said, staff effectively take a pay cut, and some leave before the price recovers.
Ghodsi also said he believes AI has already reached artificial general intelligence, by the definition his Berkeley lab used around 2010. He put the risk of AI wiping out humanity close to zero, and named cyberattacks as the real danger.
“I think the cyber risk is real and really bad things can happen with that,” he said.
