articles.title: 5 clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player - Engadget
articles.text:
5 clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player
If you don't have discs to play, they can make for clever fodder for DIY projects.
Old tech has a way of hanging around. You might have a drawer of chargers and cables from outdated devices, or a box of your former phones. There could even be a laptop or two tucked away in a closet. In the age of streaming services, you might also have an old CD or DVD player collecting dust somewhere in your home.
Luckily, enterprising folks on the internet have been working on creative ways to repurpose old CD and DVD players, or at least parts of them, and turn them into a variety of projects. These DIY efforts range in their level of difficulty and skill required to produce. But, if you're handy and already comfortable with electronics, you might glean some inspiration and finally give that old DVD or CD player some new life.
Plus, tackling one of these projects might be another way to keep old electronics out of the landfill and cut down on the amount of e-waste you're producing. Here are five clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player.
Make a macro lens for your phone
If you're into photography, there's a relatively easy way to turn the lens from an old DVD player into a macro lens you can use on your phone. Macro photography shows small subjects up close, like a bumblebee on a flower. While this particular tutorial might not get you into the pages of National Geographic, it could be a fun way to play around with what you shoot.
YouTuber Raj K Photo shows how to use a screwdriver and adhesive putty to get the job done. It's as simple as prying out the lens, and wrapping a thin coil of putty around the lens to affix it to your phone's camera. The video notes that you have to get pretty close to the subject to get in focus, but the lens is powerful enough to see the cell structure of a layer of onion and the dirt and grooves on a coin.
Create a beginner robot
If you or someone you know is interested in robotics, but isn't exactly ready to join Boston Dynamics, there are more than a few tutorials online that will show you how to use the motors inside a device like a DVD or CD player to build a simple robot. For example, Blackfish, which offers tutorials and templates for projects, has a template for a cardboard robot who can walk around using a DC motor, an on-off switch, a plastic pulley and a battery. While you might have to purchase the pulley, switch and battery, you can find a DC motor inside your CD or DVD player. Blackfish Space has a video, too, that walks you through assembly.
There's also a tutorial from the YouTube account GrandadIsAnOldMan, which shows how to take the drive from a DVD player and create what he calls an Inchworm CrawlerBot. Essentially, the CrawlerBot uses the motion of the tray opening and closing, driven by its motors, to move itself while on wheels. This project requires a few more parts than the walking robot project, like four VHS cassette spools (in case you're old enough to have those lying around, too), barbecue skewers, a toggle switch, a hot glue gun and a soldering iron, to name a few. He also links to two other iterations of the CrawlerBot.
Construct a CNC laser engraver
On the more complicated end of the DIY spectrum, you can use old CD and DVD players to make your own CNC laser engraver of varying sizes. A CNC laser engraver is a machine that can etch, carve or mill on a hard surface like wood, metal or glass, using digital instructions. You might use this method to put a custom image or text on something.
In particular, Autodesk Instructables features YouTuber How To Do's 8-step guide to making one such CNC laser engraver, which uses two optical drives from either a CD or DVD player, as well as an Arduino board, which is an "open-source electronics platform" that will serve as the "brain" of the machine, according to the instructions. In the video description on YouTube, you can see a list of materials with links. Since the video is about 9 years old, not all the links might work. You also might note that the creator uses more than a few shop tools. He says that in reality, if you want a CNC laser engraver, you can just buy one — it'll be cheaper and easier. But undertaking this project is, as they say, about the journey.
Build a secret compartment
If you're looking to hide some personal items from prying eyes, you can turn a DVD or CD drive into a motorized drawer. Kipkay on YouTube offers a video on how to do it. You'll need a drive, a 3-volt button cell battery and holder, a magnetic switch (Kipkay mentions getting one from an old alarm system), a strong neodymium magnet, a small wire, and some type of glue.
Part of the process involves removing the guts of the drive. Along the way, you can save some components like the laser diode for other projects. Ultimately, the magnet is what will trigger the switch, opening your new secret stash drawer. The drawer can even be attached somewhere like under a desk. You won't be storing large items, but Kipkay suggests there's room for things like cash and SD cards. You can also read the directions on Instructables.
Collect spare parts
Even if you don't have a specific project in mind, you can still take apart an old CD or DVD player and harvest useful parts to use in the future. Instructables, once again, comes through with directions describing what you can salvage and how, via the YouTube account Prajjwal Nag. The instructions note that aside from saving money on parts, the act of disassembling can help you learn how the electronics work.
Among the parts you can reuse from these older devices are DC motors, stepper motors, buttons, LED lights, laser diodes, neodymium magnets, and optical lenses. To retrieve all those bits, you'll need a screwdriver, tweezers, needle-nose pliers, wire cutters and rubber gloves. Instructables also links to projects using some of those parts if you're looking for inspiration.
So, if you're wanting something to do with old CD or DVD players that doesn't just involve throwing them out, (and maybe have a quiet Saturday afternoon) you've got options for turning your old tech into something new and useful.

articles.title: The game of the year is finally here
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 153, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, thank you for tearing yourself away from GTA to be here, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The game of the year is finally here
Plus, in this week’s Installer: A better YouTube Kids, new ways to get stuff done, the FTX story on Netflix, and more.
This week, I’ve been reading about nuclear radiation and F1 brains and phone scammers, watching about 10 minutes of Madden before bailing, playing a lot of Madden NFL instead, learning my way around Instagram Edits on the Mac, trying the 12-3-30 workout while watching Mission: Impossible movies in half-hour increments, getting my new Apple HomeView up and running (still don’t know why I bought one…), and dreaming up stuff to do with the Flipper One.
I also have for you the game of the year (decade? century?), a couple of great new productivity tools, a Netflix take on the FTX story, and much more. But mostly, it’s GTA week. Let’s do it.
Also, programming note: Installer is off next week. It’s Thanksgiving, there’s food to eat and football to watch. Hope you have a great couple of weeks, and we’ll be so back in December.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / listening to / playing / adding to your holiday lists this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Grand Theft Auto VI. I mean, this literally could be the whole newsletter. But it appears this game is everything we’ve been waiting for, and I anticipate spending too much of the rest of my life playing it. No regrets.
- The GTA VI soundtrack. I can’t think of many games whose soundtracks have this kind of power: It’s a 34-song compilation, including a bunch of new music from huge artists. I’m going to listen to this while I work, which I assume will make all my writing cooler and more crime-filled.
- The Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1. I’ve been thinking about rebooting my physical media collection, and I can’t think of a better way to start than with this beautiful CD player. Like all Teenage Engineering gear, it is somehow retro and futuristic at the same time, and it’ll slide neatly into a synth setup or just look extremely rad in your living room.
- Alfred 6. A long-awaited update to the launcher and workflow tool so many Mac users love. I see some nice interface changes here but otherwise not a massively different product… but that’s actually probably the right call. Alfred is very good at being Alfred.
- The TRMNL Frame. A 31.5-inch, programmable color E Ink screen that you can hang on your wall. This either immediately excites you, and $1,299 is a small price to pay, or does nothing for you and is way too expensive. I accept both reactions equally. I also want one so badly.
- Tasks in Gemini. A stupid, stupid, stupid name for an otherwise useful product! Gemini now has a lot of the same “do stuff for you” tools that Muse and Dots offer — this time with much better access to your Google data. I’m slowly working through my inbox with this one.
- Who Wants This? Fun new podcast in which two writers and comedians attempt to make sense of current trends, and whether anyone actually… wants this. The first episode is about protein and proteinmaxxing, and I both enjoyed the hang and learned a lot. It also made me feel like everyone has just completely lost their minds.
- The Altruists. We are due for many, many fictionalized versions of the FTX story. I’ve heard and read some mixed things about this new Netflix series, but I dig the idea of trying to play it as both a love story and a scam story. It really is both those things!
- ClockwiseTV. Respect to Hank Green for being one of the few people bold enough to try and compete with YouTube. The pitch here is smart and simple: curated content for kids, on a timer, no ads, no autoplay. This is immediately going on all my iPads.
- “CIA Meeting Cold Open.” Last week’s SNL was really good overall (though maybe I just love John Mulaney?) but the cold open, with the tech billionaires learning how not to fall for a honeypot, absolutely slayed me. The spray bottle on Elon Musk makes me laugh every single time.
You may not know Tom Hovey, but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show. His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.
I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he said, “but never ever AI.”
I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: iPhone 17 Pro.
The wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.
The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.
Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.
Six apps for my kids’ primary school is too many apps.
I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!
iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a new country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.
I also asked Tom to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- I listen to a lot of audiobooks while I’m at my desk drawing and also while running, and audiobooks are the only way I can “read” non-fiction as I just fall asleep immediately if I try and actually read them. Some recent audiobooks I’ve enjoyed: The Castle by Jon Ronson; Thirst: Twelve Drinks That Changed My Life by John Robins; Hidden Valley Road by Robert Kolker; London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe.
- TV shows I’ve recently watched: The Pitt, Widow’s Bay, This Is a Gardening Show, East of Eden, Star City, Pluribus.
- As an illustrator I’m always looking for excellent people making cool things and in a world where AI art is taking over I am seeking more and more analog art so here are some of the coolest creatives I’m currently enjoying: Natalie Andrewson, Sean Morris, Carla Adams, Ellis Parrinder, Azpeger Tat, and Kawafi.
- I have a WhatsApp chat with a bunch of my old illustrator pals which is a bunch of old men gossiping and sending each other Paul McCartney memes.
- Really enjoying the internet’s response to Damian Lewis’s foray into music.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Forget GTA VI, the game of the year is Queen’s Domain. It is only $20 instead of $80, made by two people instead of an army. It is all I have been playing this week.” — Mike
“In Meg Elison’s new novel, Foundling Fathers, some creepy tech billionaires clone Washington Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams and try to raise them in an ‘originalist’ setting. The satire is hilarious and all too plausible.” — aAron
“I’m not playing with it yet myself, but the FM-1 from M-Vave seems to be capturing the first wave of post-vibe-coding synthesized nerds, who are all replacing the stock firmware with homebrew. So a cheap Chinese generic keyboard is suddenly really hot hardware even though it’s like $50.” — Anil
“Reading John Scalzi’s The Kaiju Preservation Society and it is simple, honest sci-fi fun. Classic Scalzi.” — 4nd3rs
“Stick on Apple TV got me through the week until GTA VI!” — Justin
“Claude and I went around this week with a tape measure and built a to-the-inch accurate 3D model and floorplan of our house, which inevitably led to making it a Doom map.” — Michael
“I switched to ReadKit on my Mac and iPhone now that it has iCloud-based RSS sync.” — Todd
“Recently found the book The Canceling of the American Mind by Greg Lukianoff and Rikki Schlott at my local library. It is a well-written investigation into the effects of cancel culture on public debate and education. Wherever you fall on the political spectrum, this book will challenge you to think about how we should engage with ‘dangerous’ and ‘offensive’ ideas.” — Josh
“Been watching From since the first three seasons are available on Netflix right now. It’s a good show, has very Lost vibes to it.” — Bobby
Signing off
One of the most underrated strange things about the tech industry is how much The Social Network changed the way people think about Mark Zuckerberg. Yes, the movie takes huge liberties, and yes, every single person involved with the movie was quick to remind us that it was fiction. But for so many people, Jesse Eisenberg’s character just became who Zuck was.
I think Andrew Garfield in Artificial might be about to do the same thing to Sam Altman. The new trailer looks fabulous, all the early buzz about the movie seems to be great, and the movie absolutely could not be more perfectly timed. It’s apparently a pretty brutal look at Altman, OpenAI, and the whole AI movement — I wonder how Garfield and his handsomeness might bend the way the world responds. I cannot wait to see this movie.
See you in two weeks!

articles.title: Cognition funding talks value the Devin maker at $75bn
articles.text:
Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, is in talks to raise money at a $75bn valuation, two months after its last round. Bloomberg’s Rebecca Torrence reported the talks on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The company is weighing a raise of $2bn or more, according to Bloomberg. The talks are ongoing and the details could change. TNW has not independently verified the report.
Existing investors lead the interest
Most of the interest has come from current backers, Bloomberg reported. Avenir, Accel, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Lux Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners are in talks to take part, some of the people said.
Avenir, Accel and Lux declined to comment to Bloomberg. Bessemer, Lightspeed and Cognition did not respond to its requests.
A completed deal would be Cognition’s third round this year. It has already raised more than $3bn in 2026, including over $2bn at a $48bn valuation in September. That round nearly doubled its value in 15 weeks, after a $26bn round in May.
The figure sits inside the range reported last month. In October, Business Insider’s Katie Roof reported investor offers valuing Cognition at $70bn to $80bn.
A crowded race in AI coding
Investors have poured money into startups building AI agents for software work. Devin competes with Cursor, which SpaceX bought for $60bn. Days after that deal closed, SpaceX reportedly approached Cognition about a takeover too.
Cognition sells to companies including Citigroup and Nvidia. In September it said it was on track for $1bn in annualised revenue, roughly double its run rate four months earlier. This month it signed an alliance with McKinsey to sell Devin to large firms.
The size of the raises has drawn criticism. Ed Zitron, a critic of the AI industry’s spending, questioned the round on X.
“Why does this company need $5bn in the space of a year,” Zitron wrote.

articles.title: Waymo recalls robotaxis after they drove into closed freeway lanes - Engadget
articles.text:
Waymo recalls robotaxis after they drove into closed freeway lanes
The recalls come after the California DMV banned Waymo from operating on its state freeways.
Waymo filed a pair of recalls for its robotaxi fleet following incidents where its vehicles drove into closed freeway lanes and didn't follow manual commands from emergency responders. As first reported by Reuters, the Alphabet-owned company said the two recalls were "to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control." Waymo cars will operate normally on city streets, while freeway drives remain on pause as the company works on software improvements to address the issues.
Waymo filed the recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration shortly after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its robotaxis from state freeway use. The state's DMV called the robotaxis an "imminent hazard to public safety" following a few incidents where Waymo vehicles drove into construction zones that were closed to traffic. According to the California DMV, three Waymo robotaxis entered restricted construction zones in the city of Burlingame on separate occasions. A Waymo robotaxi was also seen trying to navigate around a California Highway Patrol car that was performing a traffic break.
"Yesterday, we filed two voluntary recalls on our automated driving system to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control," a Waymo spokesperson told Engadget. "These are standard steps in our rigorous safety approach to validating and refining our technology as we scale to more complex driving environments."
Waymo said that it's still working on a remedy for the closed freeway lanes recall, but added that there were no collisions or injuries from this issue, according to Reuters. However, Waymo pushed out an update earlier this month to improve how its robotaxi fleet responds to manual commands from emergency responders, following a collision involving an officer directing traffic, as reported by Reuters.
Earlier this year, Waymo recalled its robotaxis for a similar issue where they would enter freeway construction zones at speed. The company eventually resumed freeway service in the summer after identifying "an area of improvement regarding performance around freeway construction zones." Previously, Waymo filed a recall after one of its robotaxis drove into a flooded road in San Antonio, Texas.

articles.title: Trump says there could be a 'positive spin' from the latest FBI database hack
articles.text:
President Donald Trump suggested Saturday that there could be a bright spot in the latest incursion into the FBI computer database.
The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information.
The hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center (NCIC), a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW. The database is restricted to law enforcement use but not classified and it is unclear what data was extracted.
CNN had first reported on the suspected hack, citing sources familiar with the issue.
In a wide-ranging interview on Fox, Trump said there could be upside from the news.
"Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," he said. "I always like to put things on a positive spin."
This would be the second recent intrusion into the FBI system; the previous one came in September, when a group known as "ShinyHunters" broke into an FBI jobs website. The result compromised data on current and former FBI employees and shut down part of the agency's operations until the issue was resolved.
Trump said it's possible there could be information gleaned from the latest hack.
"I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?" he said. "People should hear about it, because it actually put our country in danger, and so maybe we'll learn things that we wouldn't have learned otherwise."
The FBI did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

articles.title: I never wanted the American Dream and I felt like something was wrong with me—until I moved abroad
articles.text:
I got my first job at 17, working the register at an Eckerd's drugstore in Texas. My manager was only a few years older than me, and while my coworkers seemed motivated by the idea of working their way up to his position, I felt no desire to follow that path.
It all felt suffocating: the added responsibility, the longer hours, the idea that this was the ladder I was supposed to want to climb. I wanted to work, but I couldn't wrap my head around building my whole identity around a job.
I never wanted the American Dream I saw so many people around me striving to achieve. For a long time, I wondered if something was wrong with me. It wasn't until I finally made a long-term move abroad about a decade ago that I realized it was okay to want something different.
I never dreamed about traditional milestones
After college, I got a job in travel sales. I was good at it. Talking about travel all day suited the wanderlust I'd carried since my first trip abroad in my teens.
I continued working in sales, marketing and the odd temp role for years. But they were always just jobs. I didn't feel like they defined me or feel a calling to an industry or title the way people around me seemed to.
Of course, I wanted financial stability, but I was unwilling to sacrifice my time and well-being to get it. I just didn't connect with the version of ambition that meant grinding toward a corner office. What I wanted the most wasn't status; it was freedom, growth and new experiences.
The wanderlust eventually caught up to me, and at 26 I moved to Spain to teach English. Even though I was working, people saw it as taking a year off from my career and warned me it could damage my resume. I simply didn't care. Living for my resume had never made sense to me.
Looking back, I think being abroad offered an escape from the pressure to chase the traditional path of the American Dream. There, I felt free to enjoy life and figure out who I was without worrying about what box I needed to tick next.
I wanted to stay in Spain, but I couldn't find a visa that would let me live there long-term, so I returned to the U.S. I became a serial job hopper for almost 10 years, quitting a job every year to spend summers visiting friends in the Netherlands, the U.K. and Switzerland or solo traveling in Spain on the money I'd saved up.
On the personal side, I wasn't in a rush to get married or have kids. In my 30s, single and childfree, I felt like I was failing at adulthood, even though deep down, I didn't actually want the things I was supposedly behind on. Settling down just because everyone else was doing it never felt right to me.
And I couldn't shake the dream of living in Europe. In my 20s, people mostly assumed my desire to travel was a phase. By my 30s, the conversations had shifted and I was getting pulled aside. Friends, family and colleagues all had some version of the same message: It was time to get serious and build a life in Texas.
But my gut said to try one more time. So I did.
Moving abroad helped me redefine success
In 2015, on my fourth attempt, I finally made it to Spain for good. It was scary to shake things up when everyone around me was settling down, but deep down I knew at 35, this was my chance to stop trying to conform and start building a life that felt right for me.
In my new home, the pace was slower. I quickly noticed that people actually took their vacations. Strangers at a dinner party didn't immediately ask me what I did for work. Adults in their 30s, 40s and beyond were out living full social lives. Single, childfree women my age didn't feel like an anomaly.
Living abroad didn't solve everything overnight. I still had to figure out how to support myself. But having the space to define myself professionally without constant judgment changed what felt possible.
In 2017, I launched She Hit Refresh, where I help women over 30 figure out how to move to Europe and build new lives for themselves. It's not something I could have created from anywhere else, with any other experience than my own.
In the process, I've met so many others who left corporate America behind to create something different for themselves. I've seen more women asking the same questions I spent years asking myself. Burnt out, disillusioned with hustle culture, realizing that checking all the boxes of the American Dream they grew up on didn't deliver the feeling they were promised.
We're all figuring it out together; each of us writing a version of a life that didn't fit a standard template. Moving abroad helped me understand that success, for me, was never about earning more or owning more. It was always about more ease, more time, more space, more life.
For years, I thought I was behind. I felt like something was wrong with me for wanting a different kind of life. Looking back, I just hadn't found my place yet.
Cepee Tabibian is the founder of She Hit Refresh, where she's helped over 24,000 women age 30+ plan their move abroad. Grab her free Move Abroad After 30 Guide to start planning your own move. The daughter of Colombian and Iranian immigrants, Cepee grew up in Houston, Texas, before becoming an immigrant herself in Spain. Follow her @shehitrefresh.

articles.title: Retirees face a looming deadline for required withdrawals — missing it could trigger a tax penalty
articles.text:
Every year, millions of Americans must take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by Dec. 31.
Amid the busy holiday season, it's easy to miss the year-end deadline for required minimum distributions — a mistake that can trigger a hefty IRS penalty, experts said.
"One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute," said certified financial planner Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth at Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon.
Most retirees must start RMDs from pretax accounts at age 73. The withdrawal is based on the previous year's account balances on Dec. 31, your age and an IRS "life expectancy factor."
The first annual RMD deadline is April 1 of the year after you turn 73, and future withdrawals are due by Dec. 31. If you wait until April 1 for the first one, you'll need two RMDs that year.
RMDs also apply to certain inherited IRAs if the original IRA owner reached RMD age before their death.
In 2023, more than 14.8 million taxpayers age 70 or older had a traditional individual retirement account, according to the latest IRS data. The average year-end market value of the accounts was about $330,000.
Don't miss the RMD deadline
Deferring RMDs until the last minute raises the likelihood of mistakes, such as overlooking certain retirement accounts or making withdrawal calculation errors, Canellopoulos said.
Some 7% of Vanguard investors at RMD age missed their yearly withdrawal in 2025, up slightly from 6.7% in 2024, according to a Vanguard analysis of about 400,000 RMD-age retirees with IRA balances published in December 2025.
One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute.Alex CanellopoulosDirector of wealth at Vista Capital Partners
Among those investors, the average missed RMD was $10,500 in 2025, Vanguard told CNBC.
Investors who don't take RMDs by the annual deadline may owe an excise tax to the IRS, worth up to 25% of the amount they should have withdrawn. For example, the excise tax could be up to $2,625 for a $10,500 missed RMD.
How to reduce the IRS penalty for missed RMDs
Mistakes happen, of course.
If investors miss a required withdrawal, they could reduce the penalty to 10% if they "timely corrected" the RMD within two years and file Form 5329, according to the IRS.
In some cases, the IRS could waive the penalty entirely due to "reasonable error" if investors take "reasonable steps" to fix the shortfall, according to the agency. Investors can file Form 5329 with a letter of explanation to request the waiver.
"If you don't ask, you're not going to get it," said certified public accountant Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird. "I've never heard of anybody being denied the waiver."
Charitable transfers could cover RMDs
Investors who give to charity may be skipping a specific donation strategy that can reduce or eliminate their annual RMDs, according to Lawrence Pon, a CFP and CPA based in Redwood City, California.
They can use a so-called qualified charitable distribution, or QCD, Pon said.
A QCD has a dual tax benefit: It doesn't count as taxable income and may also satisfy at least part of an investor's yearly RMD, Pon said.
The move requires a direct transfer from an investor's pretax IRA to an eligible nonprofit organization. They can donate up to $111,000 in 2026. While QCD eligibility begins at age 70½, transfers won't start counting toward RMDs until an investor reaches their RMD age.
Generally, taxpayers only get a tax break for large charitable donations if they itemize deductions on their tax returns. But QCDs still provide a tax benefit for charitable gifts when investors use the standard deduction.
QCDs "provide a real benefit if you are not itemizing [tax deductions]," said Pon.
While there's no tax deduction for QCDs, the transfer won't increase a taxpayer's adjusted gross income, or AGI. Raising AGI can cause other tax consequences, such as higher premiums for Medicare Part B and Part D.

articles.title: During Wall Street's worst week in over a year, we put money to work. What we're buying
articles.text: Stocks suffered their worst weekly declines in more than a year as Nvidia's leadership shake-up and Anthropic's debut as a public company fueled concerns about the artificial intelligence trade. The broader market S & P 500 index dropped almost 8.6% for the week, its worst weekly decline since the April 2025 tariff-induced plunge. It joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. The Nasdaq plunged 10% for the week, its worst weekly drop in more than six years. The tech-heavy index also turned negative for 2026. Friday's selling was brutal, with the Nasdaq down 5.3% and the S & P 500 down 3.7%, underscoring the growing doubts about the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure spending and lofty valuations, compounded by mounting political opposition to new data center construction following the midterm elections. The week's turmoil pushed the S & P Short Range Oscillator deep into oversold territory, prompting us to fall back on our discipline and start deploying some of our substantial cash reserves. Here's a look at three things that drove last week's market action — and the moves we made. Nvidia and Anthropic crush stocks The AI trade faced another reckoning as Nvidia's deepening sell-off overshadowed blockbuster earnings and Anthropic's initial public offering broke all kinds of records Thursday before faceplanting on Friday. Nvidia delivered another extraordinary quarter Tuesday evening, with revenue more than doubling and guidance exceeding expectations. Interim CEO Colette Kress reinforced the company's strong fundamentals in an exclusive " Mad Money " interview with Jim Cramer, emphasizing that customers and employees remain committed despite Jensen Huang's abrupt departure. The results, however, failed to restore investor confidence. Nvidia's board ruled out reinstating Huang , even as the former CEO expressed openness to returning , prolonging leadership uncertainty. " Nvidia is casting a pall on the market that's tainting everything ," Jim said Thursday on "Mad Money." In the wake of Huang's resignation, Jim had told investors sitting on big Nvidia gains to take some profits. Nvidia shares lost 23% last week, closing Friday just above $125.53 each at their lowest level since May 2025 Anthropic's record-breaking $81.3 billion IPO failed to lift the broader market. The company said Friday that underwriters exercised the "greenshoe" overallotment of shares, bringing the total amount raised to $93.5 billion. Anthropic also pulled in $26 billion in a private placement. Shares of the Claude developer sank Friday, trading just above their $83 offering price at session lows. They pared their losses, closing at about $90 for an 8.5% decline. In Thursday's debut, shares shot up to as high as $115 apiece, but only finished up 17%, just above $97. Prior to Friday, Jim argued that Anthropic's entry into the market gave investors another way to capitalize on AI, which could be furthering Nvidia's decline . 3 portfolio names deliver strong earnings Home Depot beat earnings and revenue expectations Tuesday, demonstrating continued market-share gains despite a sluggish housing market and elevated borrowing costs. The retailer also named longtime CFO Richard McPhail as its next CEO . While a subdued outlook weighed on shares, we remain confident in the company's execution and believe a potential decline in mortgage rates could fuel a housing recovery. We reiterated our buy-equivalent 1 rating and $370 price target. Rival Lowe's reported a solid quarter on Wednesday. But we still give Home Depot the edge. For the week, Home Depot lost 2.8%, but it's still up more than 20% from its most recent lows early last month. TJX Companies surged 8% on Wednesday after reporting a better-than-feared quarter . Importantly, comparable sales at the off-price retailer's largest division, Marmaxx, improved to 2% growth from 1% in the prior quarter, easing some concerns about execution issues. Marmaxx houses T.J. Maxx and Marshalls. Jim welcomed the improvement but cautioned that Marmaxx still has work to do before declaring a full turnaround. We're holding our remaining shares, maintaining our hold-equivalent 2 rating and $180 price target. With all the market turmoil, TJX rose nearly 4% for the week. Palo Alto Networks was our best performer last week, gaining 6.5%. The cybersecurity company delivered a strong quarter Wednesday evening, as AI introduces new threats and boosts demand. Palo Alto also announced a $4.5 billion acquisition of Applied Compute to expand its capabilities in securing enterprise AI models. CEO Nikesh Arora discussed the growing need for modernized cybersecurity defenses with Jim on "Mad Money." Following the stock's sharp rally, we maintained our hold-equivalent 2 rating and $400 price target. Our other cyber stock, CrowdStrike , rose 1.3% for the week. It is expected to report earnings the evening of Dec. 1. CrowdStrike shares slumped in extended trading Friday after Bloomberg News reported the company was in talks to acquire cyber rival Zscaler, which had a market cap of roughly $32 billion. Where we're putting cash to work With the S & P Short Range Oscillator finally flashing oversold conditions, we're starting to put some of our substantial cash reserves to work after weeks of market volatility. On Monday, we completed our planned semiconductor swap , exiting Intel at a roughly 50% loss and initiating a position in Advanced Micro Devices . AMD's more flexible chip designs better position it to meet booming data center CPU demand, while Nvidia's leadership uncertainty could create opportunities to gain GPU market share. AMD shares dropped 7% on Thursday after a short seller's report alleged improper China sales. The stock dropped another 13.3% on Friday. All along, Jim said he was itching to buy the dip but couldn't due to our Club trading restrictions when he mentions a stock on television. AMD pushed back on the short-seller's accusations in a statement to our CNBC colleagues Thursday . "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," a company spokesperson said. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity." We also trimmed Apple on Monday after its 31% rally this year, reducing its portfolio weighting to about 4.5% from 5.5% and locking in a roughly 1,800% gain on shares purchased in 2014. We still view Apple as an "own it, don't trade it" stock but wanted to right-size the position. When positions start to go above 5%, we tend to take some off because we aim to run a diversified book and don't want any one position to make or break the portfolio. On Thursday , we bought more FedEx Freight , encouraged by improving pricing power following its transition to a standalone company. We also added to Meta Platforms following a roughly 15% decline since our September trim. With shares trading at about 18 times 2027 earnings, we upgraded Meta to our buy-equivalent 1 rating. We added to Constellation Brands on Thursday as well, bringing its portfolio weighting to 2%. Improving beer sales, a valuation below 12 times earnings, and a dividend yield near 3% make it an attractive way to diversify beyond the AI trade. On Friday, we bought more shares of Bank of New York , taking advantage of the market's continued weakness to lower our cost basis and add dividend income. We're favoring high-quality companies outside the AI infrastructure trade, and BNY fits the bill with limited credit risk and investment banking exposure. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long NVDA, HD, TJX, PANW, AMD, FDXF, STZ, BNY. See here for a full list of the stocks.) articles.title: State and federal battle over prediction markets regulation heats up after midterms
articles.text:
The turf war between states and the federal government is intensifying after Democrats secured control of Congress and key governorships on midterm elections night.
While it was widely expected Democrats would step up oversight of the emerging, multibillion-dollar industry if they won control of Congress, the actions after the elections have come from primarily Republican-led states.
At the same time, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets — has ramped up its oversight of "mention" markets, where traders speculate on what individuals will say during a speech or broadcast. It's a type of event contract the agency has said is susceptible to manipulation.
CNBC first reported on Tuesday that the CFTC placed a hold on the certification of markets related to President Donald Trump's words in mid-November. Kalshi said it was complying with the order, but CEO Tarek Mansour said at an Axios event on Tuesday that the company disagreed with the regulatory decision.
On Thursday, the Senate passed a bipartisan bill that would ban CFTC-registered entities from listing contracts involving terrorism, assassination, war or military operations. The measure also bars contracts that are "reasonably expected" to resolve based on an individual's death.
Criminal charges, restraining order, lawsuits
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders, Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, on Oct. 28, asserting the company violated a state law that prohibits gambling.
Kalshi's founders are expected to appear in person at Utah's Third District Court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.
"This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona," said Kalshi's spokesperson Dani Lever.
In a separate, civil complaint on Oct. 20, Utah also named institutional market maker Susquehanna International Group as a defendant, along with Kalshi.
Though Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes filed a criminal complaint against Kalshi in March, a federal judge blocked the case from proceeding in April.
Louisiana's Republican attorney general also filed a complaint to ban multiple exchanges from operating in the state on Nov. 12. A state judge ordered a temporary restraining order against the prediction market companies that same day.
"Who would have thought that these red states, that were reluctant to jump into the litigation arena, ended up having the most boldest and most innovative solutions," said gambling attorney Daniel Wallach, noting that Louisiana and Utah's latest lawsuits were led by Republican attorneys general.
In response, the CFTC sued Louisiana on Nov. 13. Separately, the federal agency filed suit against Arkansas after that state pursued civil enforcement against Kalshi.
The CFTC has sued 12 states as it tries to defend what it views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate prediction markets.
Meanwhile, the CFTC may soon add commissioners. President Donald Trump sent bipartisan nominations to the U.S. Senate on Nov. 12 to fill two of the four open seats on the commission. Chairman Michael Selig has been the only member since his nomination was approved by the Senate in December 2025. 
Nathan Anonick, a Republican, and Matthew Rowland, a Democrat, appeared before the Senate Agriculture Committee on Tuesday. Multiple senators questioned them on the issue of prediction markets. Both demurred when asked whether they viewed sports-related event contracts as gambling.
Kalshi loses in Maryland
The CFTC's position faced another setback in a complicated decision by the Fourth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals this week. The court ruled 2-1 that Maryland can enforce its state gambling law against Kalshi, though the judges disagreed on the reasoning.
"Judges can't agree with each other on why we're wrong," Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said in a statement about the decision. "This splintered decision, including three separate contradictory opinions, demonstrates there is no unified coherent legal argument against prediction markets."
Overall, prediction markets have now seen three losses and one win at the circuit court level. It's widely expected the question of whether states or the federal government can regulate sports-related event contracts will be decided by the Supreme Court.
Donald Trump Jr. parts ways with Kalshi
Kalshi on Nov. 12 ended its advisory relationship with Donald Trump Jr. The prediction platform pointed to his venture capital firm 1789 Capital having a stake in rival platform Polymarket.
Though 1789 Capital announced its holding in Polymarket in August, Kalshi and the president's son ended their relationship after Democrats secured a majority in the House and Senate. Democratic lawmakers are expected to probe companies with relationships to the Trump family.
Nine Democratic senators, led by Adam Schiff, D-California, on Monday sent a letter to the CFTC asking it to reverse a directive to platforms not to geofence their offerings when they receive unfavorable court rulings stopping exchanges from operating in certain states.
Geofencing involves the use of location technology to block users in certain jurisdictions from participating in events contracts.
"Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed," the senators wrote.
Meanwhile, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, D-California, has called for Congress to ban sports-related prediction markets entirely.
"Kalshi, a $40B company, lets 18 year olds bet on sports. They call it a 'prediction market.' It's gambling," he wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. "Investigate and ban sports prediction markets."
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title: From trash to treasure: Most hated stocks are winning as AI bull market rolls over
articles.text: The artificial intelligence trade is losing steam, but investors may be able to find some stock market winners by digging deep in the dustbin. The unwind of the AI trade dragged the Nasdaq Composite to a loss on the year, now off 2.7% in 2026. The past month has been especially brutal for the tech-heavy index, which has lost 14% in the period. However, several non-AI stocks that are widely disliked by analysts may offer refuge from the tech-driven sell-off. Some of these names, such as the Campbell's Company , are touting solid gains in an otherwise rocky time for the market. "At the top of that list of what nobody 'wants' to buy is probably The Campbell's Company… who is buying canned soup outside the doomsday alarmists," BTIG chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky said in a note to clients. Just one analyst out of 23 rate Campbell's a buy, according to FactSet. Shares are up nearly 20% in the past month. Further gains could be in the cards, according to Krinsky. "Nobody owns it, and it's universally unloved," he said. "That can be a very powerful set-up, and with a 'volume pocket' up towards the $30 level, the stock can see a sharp move higher here." CNBC used FactSet data to screen for other unloved stocks in the S & P Composite 1500 that have outperformed the overall market over the past month. All of the picks have buy ratings from no more than 10% of the analysts who cover them. Clorox is one of the most hated stocks on Wall Street, with the majority of analysts rating it a hold. On average, analysts also see shares of Clorox suffering an 11% decline over the next 12 months. Despite all of that, Clorox has jumped roughly 20% over the past month. JetBlue Airways is another unpopular stock that has rallied recently. According to FactSet, just one analyst has a buy rating on the airline. JetBlue's finances have been under pressure as it contends with higher fuel costs. However, shares have risen 14% over the past month. The company has also fleshed out its new corporate strategy. Finally, Boston Beer has seen share gains as of late. The stock is up nearly 13% over the past month. The maker of Twisted Tea lifted its full-year guidance in October, calling for adjusted earnings of $9 to $10.50 per share and topping the FactSet consensus estimate of $8.90 a share. That hasn't translated to optimism on the Street, however. Just 6.7% of analysts who cover the stock have a buy rating on it, according to FactSet. Other unpopular stocks that made the list include Lululemon and Prudential Financial.

articles.title: Warren Buffett quadruples Thanksgiving gifts: A breakdown of how much wealth he's giving away
articles.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as his Thanksgiving gifts soar
Warren Buffett, 96, more than quadrupled his Thanksgiving donations to four family foundations this year to $5.5 billion.
The gifts consist of Berkshire Class B shares that have been converted from his roughly $160 billion of Class A shares.
The increase is in line with his new goal, announced last July, to give away all of his Berkshire Hathaway shares "within about eight years," with no additional annual donations going to the Gates Foundation.
Around $2.2 billion of shares goes to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named for his late first wife, with the three foundations run by his children, Susie Buffett's Sherwood Foundation, the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and Peter Buffett's NoVo Foundation each getting $1.1 billion each.
In July of last year, Buffett gave shares worth $4.6 billion to the Gates Foundation with another $1.4 billion going to the family foundations.
This July, the family foundations received $5.9 billion in stock, bringing the year's total to $11.4 billion, an increase of almost 55% from last year, even as the Gates Foundation received nothing.
In comments included in the Berkshire news release this week announcing the new gifts, Buffett reaffirmed his confidence in his children's ability to disburse his fortune over time, saying they "have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity."
He also said his confidence in Berkshire is "as strong as ever."
Recalling that in last year's lengthier Thanksgiving message he had said, "Kindness is costless but also priceless," Buffett wrote, " A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie [Munger] and I ever bought."
"Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.
"Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I'm grateful to every one of them.
"This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."
Berkshire rally stalls but it's not as bad as S&P's AI selloff
Berkshire Hathaway's fourth quarter rally that had produced a string of record highs cooled this week as both classes of its stock posted five straight daily declines.
That sent them down 3.9% for the week.
Last Friday, Berkshire was up 19.1% since October 1. Now that gain has been cut to 14.5%
The S&P's decline of 8.6% this week, however, was even bigger than Berkshire's 5-day drop, as investors sold to lock in profits from AI-related stocks.
The benchmark index, along with the Dow Industrials, are in a correction after falling 10% from their recent highs, and the Nasdaq Composite has erased all of its year-to-date gains.
Berkshire's smaller decline increased its year-to-date outperformance of the S&P to 12.5 percentage points.
One Wall Street firm, however, thinks Berkshire's run-up has run its course.
Argus Research downgraded the B shares to hold from buy Friday, saying the stock is "fully valued" at about 25 times next year's estimate for operating earnings per share.
Berkshire buys Delta, sells BofA in quiet quarter
As foreshadowed by its 10-Q financial report released almost two weeks ago, Berkshire Hathaway's Q3 13F portfolio snapshot filed with the SEC on Monday showed it wasn't doing much buying and selling of equities this summer.
And the two largest additions, Lennar and Bending Spoons, had been previously disclosed, along with additional purchases at the start of the fourth quarter.
The most notable change we didn't expect was a 12% increase in Berkshire's Delta Air Lines position, bringing it just short of a 10% stake, now valued at $5.2 billion.
Exceeding 10% triggers a number of regulatory burdens, including the requirement to promptly disclose new buying or selling, so we may not see additional purchases going forward.
Delta's return to the portfolio after Warren Buffett sold all of Berkshire's airline stocks in 2020 has been something of a surprise given his bumpy ride with the industry over the years.
As expected, Berkshire continued to trim its Bank of America stake. After nine consecutive quarters of sales, it's been cut by 56% but remains the fifth largest portfolio holding at $21.4 billion.
Berkshire also cut another financial, Capital One, by almost 62%, although it was already a relatively small position, now worth $207 million.
Also notable are two positions that didn't change.
After adding $17 billion in Q2 to the Alphabet bet that had only been initiated last summer, Berkshire defied some expectations by keeping the holding unchanged.
Its 106 million shares are valued at $28.1 billion.
And for the fourth consecutive quarter, Berkshire's largest equity holding, Apple, didn't change. With a big boost from the stock's year-to-date gain of 26.1%, the position is now valued at more than $78 billion.

Why Buffett doesn't worry about what he eats (2001)
Warren Buffett loves to eat what many would call junk food and drink a lot of sugary beverages. A quarter-century ago, when he was 70, Buffett explained why he still thought a life insurance company would rate his life expectancy "considerably better than the average."
AUDIENCE MEMBER: Every time I hear what you like to eat, Warren, it makes me wonder what your cholesterol level is — (laughter) — or if you even worry about it...
WARREN BUFFETT: I do know the number, and I don't remember it. My doctor tells me, "It's a little high," but if he says it's a little high, it means it isn't that high, or he would — because he always tries to push me into making a few changes in my life.
But he — I've got a wonderful doctor. And I was lucky last year, because I hadn't been in to see him for about five years. And — (laughter) — due to — those guys cost a lot of money, I mean. (Laughter)
And due to purely an accident, a reaction to some other medicine I was given when I was out of the city, he got a hold of me, and then he shamed me into having a physical. And it was extremely lucky, because I had a polyp in the colon that would have probably caused trouble, you know, within a couple of years.
I would say that if you ask my doctor, he would want me to make a few changes, but he would also say that my life expectancy is probably a lot better than the average person of 70.
You know, I have no stress whatsoever. Zero. You know, I mean, I get to do what I love to do every day. You know, and I'm surrounded by people that are terrific.
So that problem in life just doesn't exist for me. You know, and I don't smoke or drink or, well, we'll end it right there. (Laughter)
And so, you know, if you were an underwriter for a life company, you would rate me considerably better than the average. You'd rate Charlie better than average, too.
And I'm sure that, you know, I could change it slightly, perhaps, on the probabilities, you know, if I change my diet dramatically or something. But it's very unlikely to happen.

articles.title: Tech outages are fueling a new doomsday economy
articles.text:
Americans are shopping like there's no tomorrow.
A spate of high-profile technology outages that grounded planes, halted email access and slowed bank transactions have left many people worried about artificial intelligence-driven cyberattacks and the state of the U.S. energy grid.
Government officials have dismissed rumors and speculation circulating online that there could be a nefarious culprit for the series of malfunctions. Despite those assurances, consumers like Sabrina Cepeda are readying for a larger-scale technology blackout or other emergency event.
In recent days, the Houston resident has purchased propane and lighter fluid for cooking and heating equipment that can be used without electricity. The mother of three also replenished her backup stockpiles of non-perishable foods, hygiene products and allergy medicine in the event that her family is homebound for several days.
"I have a way to keep my family fed, clean, hydrated, warm and safe," said Cepeda, 39. "You want to have these things and not need them, rather than need them and not have them."
The doomsday economy is catching a bid. Wall Street and retailers are taking note.
Emergency prep buying
At least half a dozen major technology outages took place in the U.S. between Nov. 12 and Nov. 17. In that time frame, spending at brands specializing in emergency products spiked about 400% compared with the same period a year prior, according to card data analyzed exclusively for CNBC by Consumer Edge.
At Ready America, which sells products like emergency survival kits, prepackaged water and high-calorie food bars, sales through e-commerce platforms have seen a roughly five-fold increase in recent days. In addition, corporate customers who keep the Vista, California-based company's supplies in their offices in case of emergency have called in to order more.
The company has rarely seen this much demand since the Covid pandemic sent Americans into lockdown more than six years ago, said Ready America President Trevyn Reese. As a result, Ready America asked its suppliers to scale up production. The family-owned business has faced a shortage of water purification tablets, and redirected shoppers to alternative offerings like prepackaged water pouches.
"With everything going on in the news right now, we've seen a large spike of people wanting to get prepared," said Reese.
While the string of outages brought power-related concerns to a boiling point, data shows that worries had been bubbling under the surface for weeks.
Shoppers began significantly ramping up buying from emergency preparedness brands late last month, according to Consumer Edge. Around that time, Fox News reported that the Pentagon was preparing U.S. military bases to operate for at least 90 days without external support. Exacerbating those fears was the ongoing war with Iran that President Donald Trump signaled could ramp back up.
Firearm trade group NSSF said that gun sales rose about 8% in October from the same month a year prior. Retailers and gun manufacturers have anecdotally reported that demand has remained elevated into November, which NSSF said can be attributed to a combination of uncertainty tied to the midterm election and the recent outages.
"If people are investing in firearms and ammunition, they're telling you very directly, with their wallet, what their priority is," said Mark Oliva, NSSF's managing director of public affairs. "You're literally investing in a product that's going to be able to protect your life and protect the lives of your family."
'Apocalyptic concerns'
Now, the doomsday talk has begun making its way to Wall Street.
Mizuho told clients on Monday that consumer worries about the outages — coupled with what the bank called "apocalyptic concerns" swirling on social media — drove shoppers to stock up on emergency supplies at Costco. As a result, Mizuho said it expects a key measure of non-fuel sales growth for Costco in November to rise above 10% for the first time since 2022.
And RBC said so-called doomsday prepping has had a "real impact" on buying behavior around the globe over recent weeks. Still, the Canadian bank reported that the trend has so far boosted sales for only a small basket of items, such as shelf-stable proteins, water purification products and dry-pantry foods.
Clients of Richard McWhorter, a private wealth advisor at SRM, have been rushing to Costco to buy goods in bulk and splurging for power generators. McWhorter said he's also fielded questions about how to prepare for a situation in which the financial system goes down.
"I've never seen anything like this in my life," McWhorter said. "There's the financial side of what I do, and then there's the psychological side. And the past two weeks have been much more psychological."
Metal dealer American Hartford Gold reported an uptick in customer inquiries this week. Company president Max Baecker said he heard from some customers that their interest in products like gold — long considered a safe-haven asset during times of turmoil — was driven by newfound concern about being overly reliant on digital financial networks following a glitch at JPMorgan Chase that affected customer transactions for several hours.
Vice President JD Vance abruptly canceled his appearance at a New York Times summit on Wednesday to attend meetings about the technology outages. A day prior, Jay Clayton, the U.S. director of national intelligence, told CNBC that the recent outages were not a cyberattack or a coordinated effort by a foreign nation.
Still, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., told CNBC on Wednesday that people were "freaked out" by the outages. Warner, who acts as the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said that the U.S. was "lucky" to have not yet seen a major AI-generated cyberattack or crisis due to AI agents going rogue.
Investors may begin pushing companies to accelerate their cybersecurity spending out of an abundance of caution around rogue AI agents following the outages, according to Macro Hive CEO Bilal Hafeez. Such a situation would be reminiscent of the antivirus software push seen during the dot-com boom, he said.
The Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) has climbed around 3% over the past two weeks, bucking the downtrend seen among AI stocks and the broader technology trade. The Nasdaq Composite on Friday fell into negative territory for 2026, putting the tech-heavy index on track for its first losing year since 2022.
The 'old-fashioned way'
To be sure, not everyone on social media has bought into the idea that they should be prepping for a doomsday scenario. In satirical videos posted on TikTok, users joked that they were gearing up by placing orders in the Starbucks drive-thru or purchasing significant quantities of alcohol.
Still, the topic appears to be on the minds of a growing number of Americans. U.S. Google searches for the term "prepping" have more than doubled when comparing the past month with the same period a year prior. On YouTube, queries for videos about "survivalism," a term describing the practice of preparing for emergencies, have soared by more than 5,000% over the same time frame.
Cepeda, the Houston mom, sees emergency prep efforts as a way to be safe rather than sorry. She's previously tapped into backup food stashes during extreme weather events like Hurricane Harvey in 2017 and Winter Storm Uri in 2021.
But this year is the first time that she's felt she needed to be prepared for a potential emergency caused by technology outages, she said. Cepeda and her husband have ensured they have enough cash on hand and fuel in their cars if there's a broader hit to the U.S. power grid, she said.
"We rely so much on technology," Cepeda said. "You need to be able to do these things the more traditional, old-fashioned way."

articles.title: Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020
articles.text:
Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar.
"This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company.
Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem.
It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge, which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020.
Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence.
That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX.
With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits.
After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025.
When going public was 'not worth it'
Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar.
"There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," said Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP. The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said.
Anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus.
For a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said.
Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to."
"At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy said. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that."
Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation."
That's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic missed its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money."
Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The company looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to use alternatives from Amazon and Google as well. Anthropic said it generated $1.72 in revenue per dollar spent on computing power in the third quarter, up from 68 cents a year earlier.
"It is true that it required lots of capital, but when you dig in and you realize that capital is going toward compute, and this is the team that's positioned to use that compute in the most effective way, then we could connect those dots," Chahal said. He added that those metrics showed it was "going to be a very high-quality business."
IPO pipeline?
Anthropic isn't the only big win for VCs this year.
Five months before Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, SpaceX hit the market in what, until this week, was by far the largest IPO in history. SpaceX, which Elon Musk founded in 2002, produced outsized returns for firms including Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz.
SpaceX and Anthropic alone will make 2026 a monster year for the venture industry, easily exceeding any other year in IPO proceeds. And investors in OpenAI hope appetite remains strong for trillion-dollar companies next year, as the ChatGPT maker is looking to 2027 for a potential offering.
IVP's Dash said that in his AI portfolio, "a lot of companies are starting IPO prep" even if it's only "year four, year five, year six since inception." He hopes to see at least half a dozen companies go public at valuations north of $10 billion each in the second half of 2027.
The macro picture, however, is ominous.
Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia has left the chip giant without a clear leader at a time when the company already faced heightened concerns about a slowdown in spending. Nvidia is a key investor in Anthropic and OpenAI and a critical supplier and financing partner for the entire AI industry, which is getting hammered across the board.
In January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after this month's midterm elections, which included the passage of numerous ballot measures that could stymie data center development. Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner predicted after the election that market dynamics would push Anthropic to price toward the lower end of its range.
Narasin said he wasn't even sure the company would get that far.
"I was concerned they'd delay," Narasin said.
That makes the outcome that much more impressive, he said, after Anthropic priced above its expected range and upsized the offering.
"This will be bedtime stories for years for future VCs," Narasin said. "There was a company that was created, backed by angels and later venture" that in a few short years "became the single biggest IPO of all history."
— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

articles.title: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.text:
The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.
U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.
Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.
It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.
The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.
A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.
"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.
The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.
"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."
There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.
A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.
American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.
Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)
Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.
American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.
"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."
No soup, no olives
Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.
On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.
First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.
And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.
"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."
Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.
American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.
Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.
Carving up business class
Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.
United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.
There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.
There's more to come.
"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."
First class still flies globally
Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.
Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.
British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.
Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.
"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

articles.title: An early breakdown in the polar vortex is threatening already depleted gas stocks
articles.text:
An unprecedented early breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex and a record-breaking El Niño event has put energy traders on alert this winter, with analysts warning the weather and climate phenomena could have an outsized impact on Europe.
Meteorologists are currently observing a record early breakdown of the polar vortex, a large-scale circulation of strong winds that typically keeps extremely cold air over the North Pole.
Changes in the strength and shape of the polar vortex can influence weather patterns much lower down in the atmosphere, potentially bringing in colder weather to parts of Europe and North America.
